theorem.raw:
Let $v_1,v_2,...,v_d$ be a family of bounded operators on a Hilbert space
${\cal K}$ so that $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$. Then there exists a unique up to
isomorphism Hilbert space ${\cal H}$, a projection $P$ on ${\cal K}$ and a family of isometries
$\{S_k:,\;1 \le k \le d \}$ satisfying Cuntz's relation so that
\begin{equation}
PS^{*}_{k}P=S_k^*P=v^*_k
\end{equation}
for all $1 \le k \le d$ and ${\cal K}$ is cyclic for the representation i.e. the vectors
$\{ S_I{\cal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal H}$.

Moreover the following holds:

\noindent (a) $\Lambda^n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ where $\Lambda(X)=\sum_k S_kXS_k^*$;

\noindent (b) For any $D \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})=\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kxv_k^*=x \}$, 
$\Lambda^n(D) \rightarrow X'$ weakly as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for some $X'$ in the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$ so that $PX'P=D$. Moreover
the self adjoint elements in the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$ is isometrically
order isomorphic with the self adjoint elements in ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ via the
surjective map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$, where ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})=\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \sum_{1 \le k \le d }
v_kxv^*_k=x \}.$

\noindent (c) $\{v_k,v^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}' \subseteq {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ and equality holds if and only if
$P \in \{S_k,S_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$.

\vskip 1em 
If $(w_i)$ be another such an Popescu elements on a Hilbert space ${\cal K}'$ such that there exists an operator 
$u:{\cal K} \rightarrow {\cal K}'$ so that $\sum_k w_kuv_k^*=u$ then there exists an operator $U:{\cal H}_v \rightarrow {\cal H}_w$ so 
that $\pi'(x)U=U\pi(x)$ where $({\cal H}_w,\pi',S'_i)$ are Popescu dilation of $(w_i)$ and $\pi'$ is the associated
minimal representation of ${\cal O}_d$. In particular $U$ is isometry, unitary if $u$ is so respectively. If $u$ is unitary 
and ${\cal K}={\cal K}'$ then we can as well take ${\cal H}_v={\cal H}_w$.

proposition.raw:
There exists a canonical one-one correspondence between the following objects:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) States $\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) Function $C: {\cal I} \times {\cal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with the following properties:

\noindent (i) $C(\emptyset, \emptyset)=1$;

\noindent (ii) for any function $\lambda:{\cal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with finite support we have
         $$\sum_{I,J \in {\cal I}} \overline{\lambda(I)}C(I,J)\lambda(J) \ge 0$$

\noindent (iii) $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_d} C(Ii,Ji) = C(I,J)$ for all $I,J \in {\cal I}$.

\vskip 1em
\noindent (c) Unitary equivalence class of objects $({\cal K},\Omega,v_1,..,v_d)$ where

\noindent (i) ${\cal K}$ is a Hilbert space and $\Omega$ is a unit vector in ${\cal K}$;

\noindent (ii) $v_1,..,v_d \in {\cal B}({\cal K})$ so that $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_d} v_iv^*_i=1$;

\noindent (iii) the linear span of the vectors of the form $v^*_I\Omega$, where $I \in {\cal I}$, is dense in ${\cal K}$.

\vskip 1em
The correspondence is given by a unique completely positive map $R: {\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$, where 

\noindent (i) $R(s_Is^*_J)=v_Iv^*_J;$

\noindent (ii) $\psi(x)=<\Omega,R(x)\Omega>;$

\noindent (iii) $\psi(s_Is^*_J)=C(I,J)=<v^*_I \Omega,v^*_J\Omega>;$

\noindent (iv) For any fixed $g \in U_d$, the completely positive map $R_g:{\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$ defined by $R_g= R
\circ \beta_g$ give rises to a Popescu system given by $({\cal K},\Omega,\beta_g(v_i),..,\beta_g(v_d))$ where
$\beta_g(v_i)=\sum_{1 \le j \le d} \overline{g^i_j} v_j.$

proposition.raw:
Let $\psi$ be a state on ${\cal O}_d$ and $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$ be the GNS space associated with 
$({\cal O}_d,\psi)$. We set $S_i=\pi(s_i)$ and normal state $\psi_{\Omega}$ on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ defined by 
$$\psi_{\Omega}(X) = <\Omega, X \Omega>$$
Let $P$ be the projection on the closed subspace ${\cal K}$ generated by the vectors $\{S^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ and 
\begin{equation}
v_k=PS_kP
\end{equation}
for $1 \le k \le d$. Then following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $\{v^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ is total in ${\cal K}$.

\noindent (b) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$;

\noindent (c) $S_k^*P=PS_k^*P$ for all $1 \le k \le d$; 

\noindent (d) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have 
\begin{equation} 
\psi(s_Is^*_J)= <\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>
\end{equation} 
and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\cal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in
the GNS Hilbert space associated with $({\cal O}_d,\psi)$. Further such a family $({\cal K},\;v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\;\omega)$ satisfying
(a) to (d) is determined uniquely up to isomorphism. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely given a Popescu system $({\cal K},v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\Omega)$ satisfying (a) and (b) there exists a unique   state 
$\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ so that (c) and (d) are satisfied.

Furthermore the following statements are valid:
\vskip 1em
\noindent (e)  If the normal state $\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ on the von-Neumann algebra
${\cal M}=\{ v_i, v^*_i \}''$ is invariant for the Markov map $\tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k
\le d} v_ixv^*_i,\;x \in {\cal M}$ then $\psi$ is $\lambda$ invariant and $\phi$ is faithful 
on ${\cal M}$.

\vskip 1em
\noindent (f) If $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ then following are equivalent:

\noindent (i) $\psi$ is an ergodic state for $({\cal O}_d,\lambda)$; 

\noindent (ii) $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) ${\cal M}$ is a factor.

proposition.raw:
Let $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$ be the GNS representation of a $\lambda$ invariant state 
$\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ and $P$ be the support projection of the normal state $\psi_{\Omega}(X)=<\Omega,X\Omega>$ in the 
von-Neumann algebra $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. Then the following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $P$ is a sub-harmonic projection for the endomorphism $\Lambda(X)=\sum_k S_kXS^*_k$ on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$
i.e. $\Lambda(P) \ge P$ satisfying the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) $PS^*_kP=S^*_kP,\;\;1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (iii) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$ 

where $S_k=\pi(s_k)$ and $v_k=PS_kP$ for $1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have $\psi(s_Is^*_J) =
<\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>$ and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\cal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal H}$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (c) The von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}=P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P$, acting on the Hilbert space
${\cal K}$ i.e. the range of $P$, is generated by $\{v_k,v^*_k:1 \le k \le d \}''$ and the normal state
$\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ is faithful on the von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}$.

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (d) The self-adjoint part of the commutant of $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ is norm and order isomorphic to the space
of self-adjoint fixed points of the completely positive map $\tau$. The isomorphism takes $X' \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$
onto $PX'P \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$, where ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K}) = \{ x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \tau(x)=x \}$ and 
$\tau(x)=\sum_kv_kxv^*_k,\;x \in {\cal B}({\cal K})$. Furthermore ${\cal M}' = {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Conversely let ${\cal M}$ be a von-Neumann algebra generated by a family $\{v_k: 1 \le k \le d \}$ of bounded operators
on a Hilbert space ${\cal K}$ so that $\sum_kv_kv_k^*=1$ and the commutant 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal M}'=\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \sum_k v_kxv_k^*=x \}
\end{equation} 
Then the Popescu dilation $({\cal H},P,S_k,\;1 \le k \le d)$ described in Theorem 2.1 satisfies the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) For any faithful normal $\tau-$invariant state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ there exists a state $\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ defined by
$$\psi(s_Is^*_J)=\phi(v_Iv^*_J),\;|I|,|J| < \infty $$
such that the GNS space associated with $({\cal M},\phi)$ is the support projection
for $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ satisfying (a)-(d). 

\vskip 1em
Further for a given $\lambda$-invariant state $\psi$, the family $({\cal K},{\cal M},v_k\;1 \le k \le d,\phi)$ satisfying (a)-(d) 
is determined uniquely up to unitary conjugation. 

\vskip 1em
\noindent (e) $\phi$ is a faithful normal $\tau$-invariant state on ${\cal M}$. Furthermore the following statements are equivalent:

\noindent (i) $({\cal O}_d,\lambda,\psi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (iii) ${\cal M}$ is a factor.

proof.raw:
Following Popescu [Po] we define a completely positive map
$R: {\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$ by
\begin{equation}
R(s_Is^*_J)=v_Iv^*_J
\end{equation}
for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$. The representation $S_1,..,S_d$ of ${\cal O}_d$ on ${\cal H}$ thus may be taken to be the Stinespring
dilation of $R$ [BR, vol-2] and uniqueness up to unitary equivalence follows from uniqueness of the Stinespring
representation. That ${\cal K}$ is cyclic for the representation follows from the minimality property of the Stinespring
dilation. 

\vskip 1em 
For (a) let $Q$ be the limiting projection of $\Lambda^n(P)$ as $n \uparrow \infty$. Then we have $\Lambda(Q)=Q$ i.e. $Q\Lambda(I-Q)Q=0$ 
and so $(I-Q)S_k^*Q=0$. Interchanging the role of $Q$ with $I-Q$, we get $QS_k^*(I-Q)=0$. This shows $QS_k^*=S_k^*Q$ for all $1 le k \le d$. 
Since $Q$ is a projection, taking adjoint in the relation, we get $Q \in \{S_k,S^*_k\}'$. That $Q \ge P$ is obvious since $\Lambda^n(P) \ge P$ 
for all $n \ge 1$. In particular $QS_If=S_If$ for all $f \in {\cal K}$ and $|I| < \infty$. Hence $Q=I$ by the
cyclicity of ${\cal K}$. 

\vskip 1em 
For (b) essentially we deffer from the argument used in Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. We fix any $D
\in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ and note that $P\Lambda_k(D)P=\tau_k(D)=D$ for any $k \ge 1$. Thus for any integers $n > m$
we have
$$\Lambda_m(P)\Lambda_n(D)\Lambda_m(P)=\Lambda_m(P\Lambda_{n-m}(D)P)=\Lambda_m(D)$$
Hence for any fixed $m \ge 1$ limit $<f,\Lambda_n(D)g>$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ exists for all
$f,g \in \Lambda_m(P)$. Since the family of operators $\Lambda_n(D)$ is uniformly bounded and $\Lambda_m(P) \uparrow I$
as $m \rightarrow \infty$, a standard density argument guarantees that the weak operator limit of $\Lambda_n(D)$ exists as
$n \rightarrow \infty$. Let $X'$ be the limit. So $\Lambda(X')=X'$, by Cuntz's relation, $X' \in \{S_k,S^*_k:1 \le k \le k \}'$.
Since $P\Lambda_n(D)P=D$ for all $n \ge 1$, we also conclude that $PX'P=D$ by taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$. Conversely,
it is obvious that $P\{ S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P \subseteq {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$. Hence
we can identify $P\{S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P$ with ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Further it is obvious that $X'$ is self-adjoint if and only if $D=PX'P$ is self-adjoint ( since $\Lambda^n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, 
by taking limit $\Lambda^n(PXP)=\Lambda^n(PX^*P)$ shows that $X^*=X$ if $D^*=D$ ). Now fix any self-adjoint element $D \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$. Since 
the identity operator on ${\cal K}$ is an element in ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ for any $\alpha \ge 0$ for which $- \alpha P  \le D \le \alpha P$, we have $\alpha 
\Lambda_n(P) \le \Lambda_n(D) \le \alpha \Lambda_n(P)$ for all $n \ge 1$. By taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$ we
conclude that $- \alpha I \le X' \le \alpha I$, where $PX'P=D$. Since operator norm of a self-adjoint element $A$
in a Hilbert space is given by
$$||A||= \mbox{inf}_{\alpha \ge 0}\{\alpha: - \alpha I  \le A \le \alpha I \}$$
we conclude that $||X'|| \le ||D||$. That $||D||=||PX'P|| \le ||X'||$ is obvious, $P$ being a
projection. Thus the map is isometrically order isomorphic taking self-adjoint elements of the commutant
to self-adjoint elements of ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
We are left to prove (c). Inclusion is trivial. For the last part, we assume first that $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$. For any element $D$
in ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d\}'$ so that $PX'P=D$. Since $P$ commutes with $X'$, 
we verify that 
$$Dv^*_k= PX'PS^*_kP=PX'S^*_kP=PS^*_kX'P=PS^*_kPX'P=v^*_kD$$ 
We also have $D^* \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ and thus $D^*v^*_k=v^*_kD^*$. Hence $D \in \{v_k,v^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$. Since $P\pi_{\hat{\omega}}
({\cal O}_d)'P = {\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau}$, we conclude that ${\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M}'$. Thus equality holds whenever
$P \in \{S_k,S_k^*,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$. 

\vskip 1em 
For the converse note that by commutant lifting property self-adjoint elements
of the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}'$ is order isometric with the algebra ${\cal M}'$ via the map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$.
Hence $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}''$ by Proposition 4.2 in [BJKW]. 

\vskip 1em 
For the proof of intertwining relation and their property we refer to main body of the proof of 
Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW].

proof.raw:
We fix a state $\psi$ and consider the GNS space  $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$
associated with $({\cal O}_d,\psi)$ and set $S_i=\pi(s_i)$. It is obvious 
that $S^*_kP \subseteq P$ for all $1 \le k \le d $, thus $P$ is the minimal subspace 
containing $\Omega$ and invariant by all $\{ S^*_k;\;1 \le k \le d \}$ i.e.
\begin{equation}
PS^*_kP=S^*_kP
\end{equation}
Thus $v^*_k=PS^*_kP=S_k^*P$ and so $\sum_k v_kv^*_k = \sum_k PS_kS^*_kP= P$ which is 
identity operator in ${\cal K}$. This completes the proof of (a) (b) and (c).

\vskip 1em
For (d) we note that
$$\psi(s_Is^*_J)$$
$$=<\Omega, S_IS^*_J\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega,PS_IS^*_JP\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>.$$
Since ${\cal H}$ is spanned by the vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega:|I|,|J| < \infty \}$ and
${\cal K}$ is spanned by the vectors $\{ S^*_J\Omega=v^*_J\Omega:|I| < \infty \}$, 
${\cal K}$ is cyclic for $S_I$ i.e. the vectors $\{ S_I{\cal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ spans 
${\cal H}$. Uniqueness up to isomorphism follows as usual by total property of vectors 
$v^*_I\Omega$ in ${\cal K}$. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely for a Popescu's elements $({\cal K},v_i,\Omega)$ satisfying (a) and (b), we consider
the family $({\cal H},S_k,\;1 \le k \le d,P)$ of Cuntz's elements defined as in
Theorem 2.1. We claim that $\Omega$ is a cyclic vector for the representation $\pi(s_i) \rightarrow
S_i$. Note that by our construction vectors $\{S_If,f \in {\cal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ are total
in ${\cal H}$ and $v^*_J\Omega=S^*_J\Omega$ for all $|J| < \infty$. Thus by our hypothesis that
vectors $\{v^*_J\Omega:|I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal K}$, we verify that
vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega: |I|,|J| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal H}$. Hence $\Omega$ is a cyclic for
the representation $s_i \rightarrow S_i$ of ${\cal O}_d$.

\vskip 1em
We are left to prove (e) and (f). It simple to note by (d) that $\psi \lambda=\psi$ i.e.
$$\sum_i <\Omega,S_iS_IS^*_JS^*_i\Omega>= \sum_i <\Omega,v_iv_Iv^*_Jv^*_i\Omega> $$
$$=<\Omega,v_Iv_J^*\Omega> = <\Omega,S_IS^*_J\Omega>$$ for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$ where 
in the second equality we have used our hypothesis that the vector state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ 
is $\tau$-invariant. In such case we aim now to show that $\phi$ is faithful on ${\cal M}$. To that end 
let $p'$ be the support projection in ${\cal M}$ for $\tau$ invariant state $\phi$. Thus $\phi(1-p') = 0$ 
i.e. $p'\Omega=\Omega$ and by invariance we also have $\phi(p'\tau(1-p')p')=\phi(1-p')=0$. Since $p'\tau(1-p')p' \ge 0 $ and an element in 
${\cal M}$, by minimality of support projection, we 
conclude that $p'\tau(1-p')p'=0$. Hence $p'\Omega=\Omega$ and $p'v^*_kp'=v^*_kp'$ for all $1 \le k \le d$. 
Thus $p'v^*_I\Omega=v^*_I\Omega$ for all 
$|I| < \infty$. As ${\cal K}$ is the closed linear span of the vectors $\{ v_I^*\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$, we conclude 
that $p'=p$. In other words $\phi$ is faithful on ${\cal M}$. This completes the proof for (e).

\vskip 1em
We are left to show (f) where we assume that $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$. $\Omega$ being a cyclic vector for $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, the weak$^*$ limit of the increasing 
projection $\Lambda^k(P)$ is $I$. Thus by Theorem 3.6 in [Mo1] we have $(\pi({\cal O}_d)'',\Lambda,\psi_{\Omega})$ is ergodic if and only if the reduced dynamics 
$({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic. For the last part of the statement, we need to show for a projection $e \in {\cal M}$, $\tau(e)=e$ if and only if $e \in {\cal M} \bigcap {\cal M}'$.
It is an easy consequence since $\tau(e)=e$ says that $e\tau(I-e)e=0$ and so $(1-e)v_k^*e=0$. Changing the role of $e$ by $I-e$, we also get $ev_k^*(I-e)=0$ for
all $1 \le k \le d$. Thus we get that $e$ commutes with each $v_k$. $P$ being in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, $v_k \in {\cal M}$. So $e \in {\cal M}'$. Thus by a standard theorem [La,Ev,Fr,BJKW] 
ergodic property is equivalent to factor property of ${\cal M}$.

proof.raw:
$\Lambda(P)$ is also a projection in $\pi_{\psi}({\cal O}_d)''$ so that
$\psi_{\Omega}(\Lambda(P))=1$ by invariance property. Thus we have $\Lambda(P) \ge P$ i.e.
$P\Lambda(I-P)P=0$. Hence we have
\begin{equation}
PS^*_kP=S^*_kP
\end{equation}
Moreover by $\lambda$ invariance property we also note that the faithful normal state
$\phi(x)=<\Omega,x\Omega>$ on the von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}=P\pi_{\psi}({\cal O}_d)''P$
is invariant for the reduced Markov map [Mo1] on ${\cal M}$ given by
\begin{equation}
\tau(x)=P\Lambda(PxP)P
\end{equation}
\vskip 1em
We claim that $\mbox{lim}_{n \uparrow \infty}\Lambda^n(P)= I$. That $\{ \Lambda^n(P): n \ge 1 \}$
is a sequence of increasing projections follows from sub-harmonic property of $P$ and endomorphism
property of $\Lambda$. Let the limiting projection be $Y$. Then $\Lambda(Y)=Y$ and so $Y \in
\{S_k,S^*_k \}'$. Since by our construction, the GNS Hilbert space ${\cal H}_{\pi_{\hat{\omega}}}$ is
generated by $S_IS^*_J\Omega$, $Y$ is a scalar. $Y$ being a non-zero projection, it is
the identity operator in ${\cal H}_{\pi_{\psi}}$.

\vskip 1em
Now it is routine to verify (a) (b) and (c). For the first part of (d) we appeal to Theorem 2.1. For the last part
note that for any invariant element $D$ in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ so that $PX'P=D$.
Since $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ we note that $(1-P)X'P=0$.
Now since $X' \in \{ S_k,S^*_k \}'$, we verify that $Dv^*_k= PXPS^*_kP=PXS^*_kP=PS^*_kXP=PS^*_kPXP=v^*_kD$. Since $D^* \in
{\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ we also have $D^*v^*_k=v^*_kD^*$. Thus $D \in \{v_k,v^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'={\cal M}'$. Since
$P\pi_{\hat{\omega}}({\cal O}_d)'P=
{\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau}$, we conclude that ${\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M}'$. The reverse inclusion is trivial.
This completes the proof for (d).

\vskip 1em
For the converse part: for (i), since by our assumption and the commutant lifting property self-adjoint elements of the commutant
$\{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}'$ is order isometric with the algebra ${\cal M}'$ via the map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$,
$P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}''$ by Proposition 4.2 in [BJKW]. For (ii) without loss of generality, we assume
that $\phi(x)=<\Omega,x\Omega>$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$ and $\Omega$ is a cyclic and separating vector for ${\cal M}$.
( otherwise we set state $\psi(s_Is^*_J)=\phi(v_Iv_J^*)$ and consider its GNS representation )
We are left to show that $\Omega$ is a cyclic vector for the representation $\pi(s_i) \rightarrow S_i$. To that end 
let $Y \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$ be the projection on the subspace generated by the vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega:  
|I|,|J| < \infty \}$. Note that, $P$ being an element in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, $Y$ also commutes with all the elements of 
$P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P=P {\cal M} P$. Hence $Yx\Omega=x\Omega$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$. Thus $Y \ge P$.  
Since $\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ by our construction, we conclude that $Y=\Lambda_n(Y) 
\ge \Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$. Hence $Y=I$. In other words
$\Omega$ is cyclic for the representation $s_i \rightarrow S_i$. This completes the proof for (ii). 

\vskip 1em
Uniqueness up to unitary isomorphism follows as GNS representation is determined uniquely up to unitary conjugation 
and so its support projection.  

\vskip 1em
The first part of (e) we note that $PS_IS^*_JP=v_Iv_J^*$ for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$ and thus ${\cal M}=P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P$ is the von-Neumann 
algebra generated by $\{v_k,v_k^*:1 \le k \le d \}$ and thus $\tau(x)=P\Lambda(PxP)P$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$. That $\phi$ is 
$\tau(x)=\sum_k v_kxv_k^*$ invariant follows as $\psi$ is $\lambda$-invariant. We are left to prove equivalence of statements (i)-(iii).  

\vskip 1em
By Theorem 3.6 in [Mo1] the Markov semi-group $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic if and
only if $(\pi({\cal O}_d)'',\Lambda,\psi_{\Omega})$ is ergodic ( here we need to recall by (a) that
$\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). By a standard result [Ev, also BJKW] $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$
is ergodic if and only if there is no non trivial projection $e$ invariant for $\tau$ i.e. ${\cal I}^{\tau} = \{e \in {\cal M}: e^*=e,e^2=e,\tau(e)=e \}=\{0,1 \}$. 
If $\tau(e)=e$ for some projection $e \in {\cal M} $ then $(1-e)\tau(e)(1-e)=0$ and so $ev^*_k(1-e)=0$. Same is true 
if we replace $e$ by $1-e$ as $\tau(1-e)=\tau(1)-\tau(e)=1-e$ and so $(1-e)v^*_ke=0$. Thus $e$ commutes with $v_k,v_k^*$ for all $1 \le k \le d$. 
Hence ${\cal I}^{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M} \bigcap {\cal M}'$. Inequality in the reverse direction is trivial and thus ${\cal I}^{\tau}$ is trivial if and only if ${\cal M}$ is a factor. 
This shows equivalence of (ii) and (iii) follows by a standard result [La,Fr] in non-commutative ergodic theory. This completes the proof.

It is simple that $H$ is a closed subgroup. For any fix $z \in H $ we define unitary operator $U_z$ 
extending the map $\pi(x)\Omega \rightarrow \pi(\beta_z(x))\Omega$ and check that the map $X \rightarrow U_zXU^*_z$ extends $\beta_z$ 
to an automorphism of $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. For the converse we will use the hypothesis that $\psi$ is a $\lambda$-invariant 
factor state and $\beta_z \lambda= \lambda \beta_z$ to guarantee that $\psi \beta_z (X) = {1 \over n} 
\sum_{1 \le k \le n} \psi \lambda^k \beta_z(X) = {1 \over n} \sum_{1 \le k \le n} \psi \beta_z \lambda^k(X) 
\rightarrow \psi(X)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for any $X \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$, where we have used the same symbol $\beta_z$ 
for the extension. Hence $z \in H$. 

\vskip 1em
In the following instead of working with ${\cal O}_d$ we should be working with the inductive limit $C^*$ algebra and their inductive limit states. 
For simplicity of notation we still use $UHF_d,{\cal O}_d$ for its inductive limit of ${\cal O}_d \rightarrow^{\lambda} {\cal O}_d$ 
and $UHF_d \rightarrow^{\lambda} UHF_d$ respectively and so for its inductive limit states.   

\vskip 1em
Now we aim to prove (b). $H$ being a closed subgroup of $S^1$, it is either entire $S^1$ or a finite subgroup 
$\{exp({ 2i \pi l \over k})|l=0,1,...,k-1 \}$ where the integer $k \ge 1$. If $H=S^1$ we have nothing to prove 
for (b). When $H$ is a finite closed subgroup, we identify $[0,1)$ with $S^1$ by the usual map and note that 
if $\beta_t$ is restricted to $t \in [0,{1 \over k})$, then by scaling we check that $\beta_t$ defines a 
representation of $S^1$ in automorphisms of ${\cal O}^H_d$. Now we consider the direct integral representation 
$\pi'$ defined by
$$\pi'= \int^{\oplus}_{[0,{1 \over k})} dt \pi_{|_{{\cal O}^H_d}} \beta_t $$
of ${\cal O}_d^{H}$ on ${\cal H}_{|_{{\cal O}_d^H}}\otimes L^2([0,{1 \over k})\;)$, where ${\cal H}_{|_{{\cal O}_d^H}}$ is the cyclic
space of $\pi({\cal O}_d^H)$ generated by $\Omega$. That it is indeed direct integral follows as states
$\psi \beta_{t_1}$ and $\psi \beta_{t_2}$ are either same or orthogonal for a factor state $\psi$ (see the proof of Lemma 7.4 in [BJKW] for further details).
Interesting point here to note that the new representation $\pi'$ 
is $(\beta_t)$ co-variant i.e. $\pi' \beta_t=\beta_t \pi' $, hence by simplicity of the $C^*$ algebra ${\cal O}_d$ we 
conclude that $$\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi'({\cal O}_d^{H})''^{\beta_t}$$
 
\vskip 1em
By exploring the hypothesis that $\psi$ is a factor state, 
we also have as in Lemma 6.11 in [BJKW] $I \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;) \subset \pi'({\cal O}_d^H)''$. 
Hence we also have
$$\pi'({\cal O}_d^H)''= \pi({\cal O}_d^H)'' \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;).$$ 
Since $\beta_t$ is acting as translation on $I \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;)$ which being 
an ergodic action, we have 
$$\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi({\cal O}_d^{H})'' \otimes 1$$
Since $\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' \otimes 1$, we conclude 
that $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi({\cal O}_d^{H})''$. 

\vskip 1em
A proof for the statement (c) follows from Lemma 7.12 in [BJKW]. The original idea of the proof can be 
traced back to Arveson's work on spectrum of an automorphism of a commutative compact group [Ar1].

follow by repeated application of $\tilde{S}^*_i\Omega=S^*_i\Omega$ and
the commuting property of the two representation $\pi({\cal O}_d \otimes I)$ and $\pi(I \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d)$. The last
statement (c) follows from a more general fact proved below
that the commutant of $\pi({\cal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ is
order isomorphic with the set $\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \tau(x)=x,\; \tilde{\tau}(x)=x \}= \{zI: z \in  \mathbb{C} \}$ via the 
map $X \rightarrow PXP$ where $X$ is the weak$^*$ limit of $\{\Lambda^m\tilde{\Lambda}^n(x)$ as $(m,n) \rightarrow 
(\infty,\infty)$. For details let $Y$ be the strong limit of increasing sequence of projections 
$(\Lambda \tilde{\Lambda})^n(P)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Then $Y$ commutes with $S_i\tilde{S}_j, S^*_i\tilde{S}^*_j$ 
for all $1 \le i,j \le d$. As $\Lambda(P)) \ge P$, we also have $\Lambda(Y) \ge Y$. Hence $(1-Y)S_i^*Y=0$. As $Y$ commutes

Let $x \in {\cal B}({\cal K})$ so that $\tau(x)=x$ and $\tilde{\tau}(x) = x $ then as in the proof of Theorem 2.1

proof.raw:
$P$ being the support projection by Proposition 2.4 we have $\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): 
\sum_k v_k x v_k^*= x\} = {\cal M}'$. That $({\cal M}',\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is ergodic follows from a general 
result [Mo1] ( see also [BJKW] for a different proof ) as $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic for a factor state
$\psi$ being an extremal element in $K_{\omega'}$ (Proposition 2.6). Hence $\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \tau(x)=\tilde{\tau}(x)=x \} = \mathbb{C}$. Hence by 
Proposition 3.1, we conclude that $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)''= {\cal B}(\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H})$. That both $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ 
and $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ are factors follows trivially as $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)''={\cal B}(\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H})$ 
and $\pi({\cal O}_d)'' \subseteq \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)'$. 

\vskip 1em
By the discussion above we first recall that $\Omega$ is a cyclic vector for the representation of 
$\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)$. Let $G = \{ z=(z_1,z_2) \in S^1 \times S^1: \beta_z \mbox{
extends to an automorphism }$ $\mbox{on}\; \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)'' \}$ be the closed 
subgroup where
$$\beta_{(z_1,z_2)}(\tilde{s}_j \otimes s_i)=z_1 \tilde{s}_j \otimes z_2s_i .$$
By repeated application of the fact that $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ commutes with $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ and 
$S_i^*\Omega=\tilde{S}^*_i\Omega$ as in Proposition 3.1 (a) we verify that $\psi \beta_{(z,z)}=\psi$ 
on ${\cal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d$ if $z \in H$. For $z \in H $ we set unitary operator $U_z \pi(x \otimes y) \Omega 
= \pi(\beta_z(x) \otimes \beta_z(y))\Omega$ for all $x \in \tilde{{\cal O}}_d$ and $y \in {\cal O}_d$. 
Thus we have $U_z\pi(s_i)U_z^*=z\pi(s_i)$ and also $U_z\pi(\tilde{s}_i)U_z^*=z\tilde{s}_i.$  By taking 
its restriction to $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ and $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ respectively we check that
$H \subseteq \tilde{H}_{\pi} $ and $H  \subseteq H_{\pi}$.

\vskip 1em
For the converse let $z \in H_{\pi}$ and we use the same symbol $\beta_z$ for the extension to an automorphism of
$\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. By taking the inverse map we check easily that $\bar{z} \in H_{\pi}$ and in fact $H_{\pi}$ is
a subgroup of $S^1$. Since $\lambda$ commutes with $\beta_z$ on ${\cal O}_d$, the canonical endomorphism $\Lambda$ defined
by $\Lambda(X) = \sum_k S_kXS_k^*$ also commutes with the extension of $\beta_z$ on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. Note that the map
$\pi(x)_{{|}_{{\cal H}}} \rightarrow \pi(\beta_z(x))_{{|}_{{\cal H}}} $ for $x \in {\cal O}_d$ is a well defined $*$-homomorphism.
Since same is true for $\bar{z}$ and $\beta_z\beta_{\bar{z}}=I$, the map is an isomorphism. Hence $\beta_z$ extends
uniquely to an automorphism of $\pi({\cal O}_d)''_{{|}_{{\cal H}}}$ commuting with the restriction of the canonical endomorphism
on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''_{|{\cal H}}$. Since $\pi({\cal O}_d)''_{{|}_{{\cal H}}}$ is a factor, we conclude as in Proposition 2.5 (a) that 
$z \in H$. Thus $H_{\pi} \subseteq H$. As $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ is also a factor, we also have $\tilde{H}_{\pi} \subseteq H$. 
Hence we have $H=H_{\pi}=\tilde{H}_{\pi}$ and $\{(z,z): z \in H \} \subseteq G \subseteq H \times H$. 

\vskip 1em
For the second part of (a) we will adopt the argument used for Proposition 2.5. To that end we first note that $\Omega$
being a cyclic vector for the representation $\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d$ in the Hilbert space $\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H} $, 
by Lemma 7.11 in [BJKW] (note that the proof only needs the cyclic property ) the representation of UHF$_d$ on $\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H} $ 
is quasi-equivalent to its sub-representation on the cyclic space generated by $\Omega$. On the other hand, by our hypothesis that $\omega$ is a 
factor state, Power's theorem [Pow] ensures that the state $\omega'$ (i.e. the restriction of $\omega$ to ${\cal B}_R$ which is identified here with $\mbox{UHF}_d$ ) 
is also a factor state on $\mbox{UHF}_d$. Hence quasi-equivalence ensures that $\pi(I \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a factor. We also note that
the argument used in Lemma 7.11 in [BJKW] is symmetric i.e. same argument is also valid for $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$.
Thus $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes I)''$ is also a factor. This completes the proof of (a). We have proved (b) 
while giving proof of (a).  


\vskip 1em
For $X \in {\cal B}(\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H})$, as $\Lambda(X)$ commutes with $\pi(\lambda(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d))''$ and
$\{ S_iS^*_j: 1 \le i,j \le d \}$ we verify by Cuntz's relation that $\Lambda(X)$ is also an 
element in the commutant of $\pi(\lambda(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d))''$ once 
$X$ is so. It is also obvious that $\Lambda(X)$ is an element in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ if 
$X$ is so. Thus $\Lambda(X)$ is an element in the commutant/centre of $\pi(\lambda(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ once $X$ is so. For the last statement consider the map $X \rightarrow S_i^*XS_i$
on $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ which is clearly onto by Cuntz relation (3). Hence 
we need to show that $S^*_iXS_i$ is an element in the commutant whenever $X$ is so. To that end note that $S_i^*XS_i S_i^*YS_i=S_i^*S_iS_i^*XYS_i=S_i^*YXS_i=S^*_iYS_iS_i^*XS_i$ since $X$ commutes with $S_iS_i^*$. 
Thus onto property of the map ensures that $S_i^*XS_i$ is an element in the commutant/centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ once $X$ is so. This completes the proof of (c) and (d).

proof.raw:
Let $E' \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ be the projection onto the subspace generated
by the vectors $\{ S_IS^*_J\tilde{S}_{I'}S^*_{J'}\Omega,\; |I|=|J|,|I'|=|J'| < \infty \}$ and $\pi_{\Omega}$ be the restriction
of the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ to the cyclic subspace ${\cal H}_{\Omega}$ generated by
$\Omega$. Identifying ${\cal B}$ with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ we check that $\pi_{\omega}$ is unitary
equivalent to $\pi_{\Omega}$. Thus $\pi_{\Omega}$ is a factor representation. 

\vskip 1em
For any projection $E$ in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, via the unitary equivalence, we note 
that $EE'=E'EE'$ is an element in the centre of $\pi_{\Omega}(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. $\omega$ being a 
factor state we conclude that $EE'$ is a scalar multiple of $E'$ and so we have
\begin{equation}
EE'=\omega(E)E'
\end{equation}
Thus we also have $EYE'=\omega(E)YE'$ for all $Y \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)'$ and so 
\begin{equation}
EE_0=\omega(E)E_0
\end{equation}
 
\vskip 1em
Since $EE'$ is a projection and $E' \ne 0$, we have $\omega(E)=\omega(E)^2$. Thus $\omega(E)=1$ or $0$. So, for such an element $E$,
the following is true:

\noindent (i) If $E \le E_0$ then either $E=0$ or $E=E_0$ i.e. $E_0$ is a minimal projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$

\noindent (ii) $\omega(E)=1$ if and only if $E \ge E_0$ 

\noindent (iii) $\omega(E)=0$ if and only if $EE_0=0$.

\vskip 1em
As $\Lambda(E_0)$ is a projection in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by our last proposition i.e. Proposition 
3.2 (c), we have either $\omega(\Lambda(E_0))=1$ or $0$. Since $\Lambda(E_0) \neq 0$ by the injective property of the endomorphism, 
we have either $\Lambda(E_0) \ge E_0$ or $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$. In case $\Lambda(E_0) \ge E_0$ we have $S^*_iE_0S_i \le S^*_i\Lambda(E_0)S_i=E_0$ 
for all $1 \le i \le d$. If so, $S^*_iE_0S_i$ being a non-zero projection in the centre of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ (Proposition 3.2 (c) ), 
by (i) we have $E_0=\Lambda(E_0)$. Thus we have either $\Lambda(E_0)=E_0$ or $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$. 

\vskip 1em
If $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0$, we have $\Lambda(E_0) \le I-E_0$ and by Cuntz's relation we check that
$E_0 \le I - S^*_iE_0S_i$ and $S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_j \le I- S^*_jE_0S_j$ for all $1 \le i,j \le d$.
So we also have $E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0 \le E_0- E_0S^*_jE_0S_jE_0=E_0$. Thus we have either
$E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0= 0$ or $E_0S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_jE_0=E_0$ as $S^*_jS^*_iE_0S_iS_j$ is an element
in the centre by Proposition 3.2 (c). So either we have $\Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^2(E_0) \le E_0$. 
$\Lambda$ being an injective map we either have $\Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^2(E_0)= E_0.$

\vskip 1em
More generally we check that if $\Lambda(E_0)E_0=0, \Lambda^2(E_0)E_0=0,..\Lambda^k(E_0)E_0=0$ for some $k \ge 1$
then either $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)=E_0$. To verify that first we check that in such a
case $E_0 \le I- S^*_IE_0S_I$ for all $|I|=n$ and then following the same steps as before to check that $S^*_iS^*_IE_0S_IS_i
\le I-S^*E_0S_i$ for all $i$. Thus we have $E_0S^*_iS^*_IE_0S_IS_iE_0 \le E_0$ and arguing as before we complete the proof
of the claim that either $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)E_0=0$ or $\Lambda^{k+1}(E_0)=E_0.$ 

\vskip 1em
We summarize now by saying that $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),..,\Lambda^{m-1}(E_0)$ are mutually orthogonal projections with $m \ge 1$ possibly 
be infinite, if not then $\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$. 

\vskip 1em
Let $\pi_k,\;k \ge 0$ be the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to the
subspace $\Lambda^k(E_0)$. The representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ is 
isomorphic to the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to $E'$ and thus
quasi-equivalent. For a general discussion on quasi-equivalence we refer to section 2.4.4 in [BR vol-1]. Since $\omega$ is a factor state, 
$\pi_0$ is a factor representation. We claim now that each $\pi_k$ is a factor representation. We fix any $k \ge 1$ and let $X$ be an element 
in the centre of $\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)$. Then for any $|I|=k$, $S^*_IE_kS_I=E_0$ and so $S^*_IXS_I$ is an element 
in the centre of $\pi_0(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)$ by Proposition 3.2 (d). Further $S_I^*XS_I= S^*_IXS_IS^*_JS_J = S^*_JXS_J$ 
for all $|J|=|I|=k$. $\pi_0$ being a factor representation, we have $S^*_IXS_I= c E_0$ for some scalar $c$ independent of the multi-index we choose $|I|=k$. 
Hence $c \Lambda_k(E_0) = \sum _{|J|=k } S_JS^*_IXS_IS_J^*=\sum _{|J|=k } S_JS^*_IS_IS_J^*X= X$ as $X$ is an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)$. 
Thus for each $k \ge 1$, $\pi_k$ is a factor representation as $\pi_0$ is so.  

\vskip 1em
We also note that $\Lambda(E_0)\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0) \neq 0$. Otherwise we have $<S_i\Omega,\tilde{S}_j\Omega>=0$
for all $i,j$ and so $<\Omega,\tilde{S}_jS^*_i\Omega>=0$ for all $i,j$ as $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ commutes with 
$\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$. However $\tilde{S}^*_i\Omega=S^*_i\Omega$ and $\sum_i \tilde{S}_i\tilde{S}^*_i=1$ 
which leads a contradiction. Hence $\Lambda(E_0)\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0) \neq 0$. As $\pi$ restricted to 
$\Lambda(E_0)$ is a factor state and both $\Lambda(E_0)$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0)$ are elements in the 
centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF})''$, by Proposition 3.2 (d), 
we conclude that $\Lambda(E_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}(E_0).$ Using the commuting property of the endomorphisms $\Lambda$ 
and $\tilde{\Lambda}$, we verify by a simple induction method that $\Lambda^k(E_0) = \tilde{\Lambda}^k(E_0)$ 
for all $k \ge 1$. Thus the sequence of orthogonal projections $E_0, \tilde{\Lambda}(E_0),...$, are also periodic with same 
period or aperiodic according as the sequence of orthogonal projections $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),...$ is. 

\vskip 1em
If $\Lambda^m(E_0)=E_0$ for some $m \ge 1$ then we check that $\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} \Lambda^k(E_0)$ is a 
$\Lambda$ and as well $\tilde{\Lambda}$-invariant projection and thus equal to $1$ by the cyclic property of 
$\Omega$ for $\pi({\cal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$. In such a case we set $V_z=\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} z^kE_k$ for $z \in S^1$ 
for which $z^m=1$ and check that $\Lambda(V_z)= \sum_{0 \le k \le m-1}z^k\Lambda(E_k)=\sum_{0 \le k \le m-1} z^k E_{k+1}= \bar{z} V_z$ 
where $E_m=E_0$ and so by the Cuntz relations we have $V^*_zS_iV_z= \bar{z}S_i$ for all $1 \le i \le d$. Following the same 
steps we also have $\tilde{\Lambda}(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$ and so $V^*_z\tilde{S}_iV^*_z=\bar{z}\tilde{S}_i$ for $ 1 \le i \le d$. 
Thus $V_z=U_z$ for all $z \in H_0 = \{z: z^m=1 \} \subseteq H$. 

\vskip 1em
Now we consider the case where $E_0,\Lambda(E_0),..\Lambda^k(E_0),..$ is a sequence of aperiodic orthogonal
projections. We extend the family of projections $\{E_k:\;k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ to all integers by 
 
$$E_k=\Lambda^k(E_0)\;\; \mbox{for all}\;\; k \ge 1$$
and
$$E_k = S^*_IE_0S_I\;\; \mbox{for all}\;\;k \le 1,\;\;\mbox{where}\;\; |I|=-k$$
We claim that the definition of $\{ E_k;\;k \le -1 \}$ does depends only on length of the multi-index 
$I$ that we choose. We may choose any other $J$ so that $|J|=|I|$ and check the following identity: 
$$S^*_IE_0S_I = S^*_IE_0S_IS^*_JS_J=S^*_IS_IS^*_JE_0S_J=S^*_JE_0S_J$$ 
where $E_0$, being an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, 
commutes with $S_IS_J^*$ as $|I|=|J|$. Further $\Lambda^k(E_0)=\tilde{\Lambda}^k(E_0)$ ensures that 
$S_I\tilde{S}_J^*$ commutes with $E_0$ for all $|I|=|J|=k$ and $k \ge 1$. Hence we also have 
$$E_{-k}=S^*_IE_0S_I\tilde{S}^*_J\tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_JE_0\tilde{S}_J$$ 
for all $|J|=|I|=k$ and $k \ge 1$. Now we claim that 
$$\Lambda(E_k) = \tilde{\Lambda}(E_k) = E_{k+1}$$ 
for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. For $k \ge 0$ we have nothing to prove. For $k \le -1$ we check that the following steps
$$\Lambda(S^*_IE_0S_I)$$
$$=\sum_j S_jS^*_iS^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'}S_iS_j^*$$
$$=\sum_jS^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'} S_jS^*_iS_iS_j^* = S^*_{I'}E_0S_{I'}$$
where we have $I=(I',i)$ and used the fact that elements $S_jS^*_i$ commutes with $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$, which are elements in the centre of 
$\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. For a proof that 
$\tilde{\Lambda}(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ we may follow the same steps as 
$E_k=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I$ where $|I|=-k$ and $k \le -1$. 

\vskip 1em
We also claim that $\{ E_k: k \in \mathbb{Z} \}$ is an orthogonal family of non-zero projections. To that end we choose any two elements
say $E_k,E_m,\;k \ne m$ and use endomorphism $\Lambda^n$ for $n$ large enough so that both $n+k \ge 0 , n+m  \ge 0$
to conclude that $\Lambda^n(E_kE_m) = E_{k+n}E_{k+m}=0$ as $k+n \ne k+m$. $\Lambda$ being an injective map we get
the required orthogonal property. Thus $\sum_{ k \in \mathbb{Z}} E_k$ being an invariant projection for both $\Lambda$ and
$\tilde{\Lambda}$ we get by cyclic property of $\Omega$ that $\sum_{ k \in \mathbb{Z}} E_k=I$. Let $\pi_k,\; k \le -1$ be the representation $\pi$ 
of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ restricted to the subspace $E_k$. Going along the same line as above, we verify that for 
each $k \le -1$, $\pi_k$ is a factor representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$. We also set $V_z= \sum_{-\infty < k 
< \infty} z^k E_k$ for all $z \in S^1$ and check that $\Lambda(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$ and also $\tilde{\Lambda}(V_z)=\bar{z}V_z$. Hence $S^1=H$ 
as $H$ is a closed subset of $S^1$. This completes the proof of (a). Proof of (b) and (c) are now simple consequence of the proof of (a).

proof.raw:
Along the same line of the proof of Proposition 2.5 (b) we get $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements 
in $\pi({\cal O}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ where factor property 
of $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ is crucial as in proof of Proposition 2.5 (b). Same holds for $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ as 
$\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ is a factor. Here we comment that factor property of $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ can be
ensured whenever $\psi$ is an extremal element in $K_{\omega'}$ (See Proposition 3.2 (a) ). 

\vskip 1em
For (b) we will first prove ${\cal I}_0={\cal I}$ if $\omega$ is pure. As by definition ${\cal I}_0 \subseteq {\cal I}$, it is enough if we show 
${\cal I}'_0 \subseteq {\cal I}'$. Let $X \in {\cal I}'_0$ i.e. $X$ commutes with $\{ U_z:z \in H\}''$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. For each $k \in \hat{H}$, $F_kXF_k$ is an element in the commutant of $F_k\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$. $\omega$ being pure each representation $\pi$ restricted to $F_k$ is irreducible and thus
$F_kXF_k = c_k F_k$ for some scalars $c_k$. Hence $X=\sum_k c_k F_k \in {\cal I}'=\{U_z: z \in H \}''$. 

\vskip 1em
For the converse we need to show that the restriction of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ to $F'_0$ is pure. Let $X$ be an element on the subspace $F'_0$ and in the commutant 
of $F'_0\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F'_0$, ( which in our earlier notation $E'$ in Proposition 3.3 ). 
Then $X$ commutes with each $F_k$ for $k \in \hat{H}$ and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes 
\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''F_k$ as $F'_0 \le F_0$ and $F_k$ are orthogonal to 
$F'_0$ for $k \neq 0$. So $X$ commutes with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and 
$\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ i.e. $X \in {\cal I}'_0$. By our assumption ${\cal I}_0={\cal I}$, we have now
$X \in {\cal I}'$ which is equal to $\{F_k: k \in \hat{H} \}''$ and so $X=cF_0$ 
for some scalar $c_0$. This shows that $F'_0=F_0$ and $\omega$ is pure.    

\vskip 1em
(c) implies (d): $\{U_z: z \in H \}$ is a commuting family of unitaries such that $\beta_z(X)=U_zXU_z^*$ and 
thus by (c) $\{U_z: z \in H \}'' \subseteq \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. Let $X$ be an 
element in the commutant of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)''$. Then 
$X$ commutes also with $\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and thus $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by (c).
Hence $X$ is an element in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ and so 
$X=\sum_k c_kE_k$ where $E_k$ are the minimal projections in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ 
given in Proposition 3.3. However $X$ also 
commutes with $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ by our assumption (c) and $\Lambda(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ for $k \in \hat{H}$.  
So $c_k=c_{k+1}$ and $X$ is a scalar multiple of unit operator. Hence (d) follows from (c). Along the same line we prove 
(c) implies (e). For a proof for (d) implies (c) and (e) implies (c), we simply apply (a).   

\vskip 1em
Now we will prove (f) and (g). That $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
a type-I von-Neumann algebra ( with completely atomic centre ) follows by a theorem of [So] once we use (c). In the proof 
of Proposition 3.3 we have proved that the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is 
$\{U_z: z \in H_0 \}''$ where $H_0 \subseteq H$. For equality in the present situation we simply use (c), as $\beta_w(U_z)=U_z$
for all $w,z \in H$, to conclude that $U_z$ is in the centre of $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 

\vskip 1em
If (c) holds then ${\cal I}_0={\cal I}$ and thus (g) follows by (b). Here we will give another proof using the same idea to prove (f). 
Let $X$ be an element in the commutant of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$, where $\pi_0$ is the factor 
representation on the minimal central projection $E_0$ defined in Proposition 3.3. Then $X$ commutes with 
$\{U_z: z \in H \}''$ and so by (c) $X$ in an element in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. 
So $X$ is in the centre of $\pi_0(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$. $\pi_0$ being a factor representation
$X$ is a scalar multiple of $E_0$. Thus $\pi_0$ is an irreducible representation and so $\omega$ is pure. 

\vskip 1em
By Proposition 3.1 we recall that $\pi'_0$ is unitary equivalent to the GNS representation of $({\cal B},\omega)$. 
Thus $\pi'_0$ is irreducible if and only if $\omega$ is pure. So for a pure state $\omega$, 
for each $k \in \hat{H}_0$, $\pi_k$ being quasi-equivalent to $\pi'_k$, $\pi_k$ is a type-I factor 
representation of $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. This completes the proof.

proof.raw:
(a) is a restatement of Proposition 3.2 (a). ${\cal E}$ ( $\tilde{{\cal E}}$ ) being the support projection of
the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ ( $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ ) and $\psi = \psi \Lambda$ we have $\Lambda({\cal E}) \ge {\cal E}$ 
and further we have ${\cal E}=[\pi({\cal O}_d)'\Omega] \ge [\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\Omega]$ and hence increasing projections in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, 
$\Lambda^n({\cal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ because $\Omega$ is cyclic for $\pi({\cal O}_d \otimes \tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ in ${\cal H} \otimes_{{\cal K}} \tilde{{\cal H}}$ 
and limiting projection being in the commutant of $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ as well i.e. since $\Lambda(Y)=Y$ implies $Y \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ by Cuntz relations.   

\vskip 1em 
We set von-Neumann algebras ${\cal N}_1=\pi({\cal O}_d)'{\cal E}$ and ${\cal N}_2=\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''{\cal E}$. By our construction we have $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)'' 
\subseteq \pi({\cal O}_d)' $ and so ${\cal N}_2 \subseteq {\cal N}_1$. Since $\Lambda^n({\cal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ in strong operator topology, 
two operators in $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ are same if their actions are same on ${\cal E}$. So (b) is true. 

\vskip 1em 
For (c) we note that $Q={\cal E}\tilde{{\cal E}} \in {\cal N}_2 \subseteq {\cal N}_1$ and claim that $Q$ is the support projection of the state $\psi$ in ${\cal N}_2$. 
To that end let $x{\cal E} \ge 0$ for some $x \in \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ so that $\psi(QxQ)=0$. As $\Lambda^k(x{\cal E}) \ge 0$ for all $k \ge 1$ and $\Lambda^k({\cal E}) \rightarrow I$ 
we conclude that $x \ge 0$. As ${\cal E} \Omega=\Omega$ and thus $\psi(\tilde{{\cal E}}x\tilde{{\cal E}})=\psi(QxQ)=0$, we conclude
$\tilde{{\cal E}}x\tilde{{\cal E}}=0$, $\tilde{{\cal E}}$ being the support projection for $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$. Hence $QxQ=0$.
As $\psi(Q)=1$, we complete the proof of the claim that $Q$ is the support of $\psi$ in ${\cal N}_2$. Similarly $Q$ is also
the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''\tilde{{\cal E}}$. This completes the proof of (c).

\vskip 1em 
Thus if ${\cal E} {\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$, we get $\Lambda^n({\cal E}){\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}} \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}})$ and 
${\cal E} \tilde{\Lambda}({\cal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}(\tilde{{\cal E}})\tilde{{\cal F}}$ and thus taking limit we get 
${\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}$ and ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. It is obvious now that $P={\cal E} {\cal F} = {\cal E} \tilde{{\cal E}}=Q$. This completes 
the proof of (d). 

\vskip 1em
As ${\cal E} \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ and $\tilde{{\cal E}} \in \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ we check that von-Neumann algebras 
${\cal M}^1 = Q \pi({\cal O}_d)'' Q$ and $\tilde{{\cal M}}^1 = Q \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d) Q$ acting on $Q$ satisfy 
$\tilde{{\cal M}}^1 \subseteq {\cal M}^{1'}$. Now we explore that $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)''= 
{\cal B}({\cal H} \otimes_{{\cal K}} \tilde{{\cal H}})$ and note that in such a case $Q\pi( \tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d )''Q$ 
is the set of all bounded operators on the Hilbert subspace $Q$. As ${\cal E} \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ and 
$\tilde{{\cal E}} \in \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ we check that together ${\cal M}^1 = Q \pi({\cal O}_d)'' Q$ and 
$\tilde{{\cal M}}^1 = Q \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d) Q$ generate all bounded operators on $Q$. Thus both ${\cal M}^1$ 
and $\tilde{{\cal M}}^1$ are factors. The canonical states $\psi$ on ${\cal M}^1$ and $\tilde{{\cal M}}^1$ are 
faithful and normal. We set $l_k=QS_kQ$ and $\tilde{l}_k=Q\tilde{S}_kQ,\; 1 \le k \le d$ and recall 
that $v_k=PS_kP$ and $\tilde{v}_k=P\tilde{S}_kP,\; 1 \le k \le d$. We note that $Pl_kP=v_k$ and 
$P\tilde{l}_kP = \tilde{v}_k$ where we recall that, by our construction, $P$ is the support projection of 
the state $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''_{|}[\pi({\cal O}_d)\Omega]$. $Q$ being the support projection of 
$\pi({\cal O}_d)\tilde{{\cal E}}$, by Theorem 2.4 applied to Cuntz elements $\{S_i\tilde{E}: 1 \le i \le d \}$, 
$\tilde{{\cal E}} \pi({\cal O}_d)'\tilde{{\cal E}}$ is order isomorphic to ${\cal M}^{1'}$ via the map $X \rightarrow QXQ$. As the projection 
${\cal F}=[\pi({\cal O}_d)''\Omega] \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$, we check that the element $Q{\cal F}\tilde{{\cal E}}Q \in {\cal M}^{1'}$. However 
$Q{\cal F} \tilde{{\cal E}}Q={\cal E}\tilde{{\cal E}}{\cal F}\tilde{{\cal E}}{\cal E}=QPQ=P$ and thus $P \in {\cal M}^{1'}$. We also check that 
${\cal M}^1\Omega={\cal M}^1P\Omega=P{\cal M}^1\Omega={\cal M} \Omega$ and thus $P=[{\cal M}^1\Omega]$. We set 
$\tilde{{\cal M}}$ for the von-Neumann algebra generated by $\{\tilde{v}_k:\; 1 \le k \le d \}$. 

\vskip 1em 
So far our analysis did not use the hypothesis on statement (e) i.e. $P=Q$. For $P=Q$, we have 
${\cal M}^1={\cal M}$ and $\tilde{{\cal M}}^1=\tilde{{\cal M}}$. By order isomorphic property 
we get (i) is equivalent to $\tilde{{\cal E}} \pi({\cal O}_d)' \tilde{{\cal E}} = \tilde{{\cal E}} \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal E}}$ 
and taking commutant again we get $\pi({\cal O}_d)''\tilde{{\cal E}} = \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)'\tilde{{\cal E}}$. Now we invoke the first 
part of the argument changing the role or using the endomorphism $\tilde{\Lambda}$ we conclude that 
$\pi({\cal O}_d)''=\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)'$. This completes the proof of (e) provided we find a independent proof for (i) 
which is not so evident and this crucial point was not noticed in the proof given for Lemma 7.8 in [BJKW].  

\vskip 1em 
Now we will analyze the representation $\pi$ of $\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d$ which is pure to prove (i). To that end we note 
since $P=Q$ by our assumption, $\Omega$ is a common cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\cal M}}$ and ${\cal M}'$.   
Thus we can get an endomorphism $\alpha: {\cal M}' \rightarrow \tilde{{\cal M}}$ defined by 
$$\alpha(y)=\tilde{{\cal J}}{\cal J} y {\cal J} \tilde{{\cal J}}$$ 
where $\tilde{{\cal J}}$ is the Tomita's conjugate operator associated with the cyclic and separating vector $\Omega$ for $\tilde{{\cal M}}$  
( i.e. for $y \in {\cal M}'$, we have ${\cal J} y {\cal J} \in {\cal M} \subseteq \tilde{{\cal M}}'$ since $\tilde{{\cal M}} \subseteq {\cal M}'$. 
Since $\tilde{{\cal J}}\tilde{{\cal M}}'\tilde{{\cal J}}=\tilde{{\cal M}}$, we have $\alpha(y) \in \tilde{{\cal M}}$ ). We note that the general theory 
does not guarantee [AcC] that the endomorphism be Takesaki's canonical conditional expectation associated with $\phi$. If so then the modular 
automorphism group $(\sigma_t)$ of ${\cal M}'$ also preserves $\tilde{{\cal M}}$. Thus $\sigma_z(x) \in \tilde{{\cal M}}$ for $-1 \le Im(z) \le 1$ 
if $x$ is an analytic element in $\tilde{{\cal M}}$. Thus we would have got ${\cal J} v_k(\delta) {\cal J} = 
\sigma_{i \over 2}(\tilde{v}_k(\delta)) \in \tilde{{\cal M}}$ where $x(\delta)$ is average of 
$\sigma_t(x)$ with respect to Gaussian measure with variance $\delta > 0$. That $\tilde{v}_k(\delta)$ 
is an analytic element follows from the general Tomita-Takesaki theory [BR1]. Since $v_k(\delta) \rightarrow v_k$ in strong 
operator topology as $\delta \rightarrow 0$ and ${\cal M} = \{v_k: 1 \le k \le d \}''$ together with 
${\cal J} {\cal M} {\cal J} = {\cal M}'$ we arrived at $\tilde{{\cal M}}={\cal M}'$. In the following we avoid this tempting 
route and aim to explore the general representation theory of $C^*$-algebras [BR1,chapter 2].   

\vskip 1em 
We claim that ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\cal M}} \subset {\cal M}'$. Then $\alpha(\tilde{{\cal M}})$ is a proper von-Neumann subalgebras 
of $\alpha({\cal M}') \subseteq \tilde{{\cal M}} $ being an into map and hence $\alpha(\tilde{{\cal M}})$ is a proper von-Neumann 
sub-algebra of $\tilde{{\cal M}}$. Now consider the Popescu elements $({\cal K},\alpha(\tilde{v}_i),\Omega)$ and its dilation 
as in Theorem 2.1. Then by the commutant lifting theorem applied to pairs 
$(\tilde{v}_i),\alpha(\tilde{v}_i)$ we find a unitary operator $U$ on $\tilde{{\cal H}}$ so that 
$U\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''U^*$ is strictly contained in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ ( Without loss of generality we can 
take the dilated Hilbert space for $({\cal K},\alpha(\tilde{v}_i),\Omega)$ to be same as $\tilde{{\cal H}}$ as there exists an 
isomorphism preserving ${\cal K}$, see the remark that follows after Theorem 2.1 ). We extend $U$ to a unitary operator 
on $\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H}$ and denote $\pi_u(x)=U \pi(x) U^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d$ which 
is unitary equivalent to the pure representation $\pi$ and $\pi_u(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$ is strictly contained in 
$\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$. Now $\pi_u$ is also an amalgamated representation over the subspace ${\cal K}$ with 
$P_u=Q_u$. Thus we can repeat now same procedure with $\pi_u$ and so on. Note that the process won't terminate in finite 
time. Our aim is to find a contradiction from this using formal set theory.  

\vskip 1em 
To that end we use temporary notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ defined in last paragraph and $\pi$ will be used for a generic representation. 
Let ${\cal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d  
\rightarrow {\cal B}(\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H} )$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. 
$\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary 
equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus given an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ we can associate two cardinal numbers $n_{\pi}$ and $n_0(\pi)$ 
and without loss of generality we assume that $H_{\pi} \subseteq n_0(\pi)H_0$ and $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}=n_0(\pi)H_0.$  $\pi_0$ being a pure representation, 
any element $\pi \in {\cal P}$ is a type-I factor representation of $\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d $. The interesting point here that $\displaystyle{\oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P} }}\pi$ 
is also an element in ${\cal P}$ with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ 
if there exists an isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have 
$U \Omega^1_{\alpha} = \Omega^2_{\alpha'}$ for some 
$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;

\noindent (C2) $n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(x)E'_2 = U n_{\pi_1}\pi_1(x) U^* $ where ${\cal E}'_2 \in n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)'$; 
 
\noindent (C3) $U\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''U^* \subset \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''E'_2$. 

\vskip 1em 
That the partial order is non-reflexive follows as $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega) \prec (\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ contradicts (C3) as $I=E_2'$. By our starting assumption that ${\cal M}' \neq \tilde{{\cal M}}$ 
we check that $\pi_0 \prec \pi_u$. Thus going via the isomorphism we also check that for a given element $\pi \in {\cal P}$ there exists an element $\pi' \in {\cal P}$ so that $\pi \prec \pi'$. 
Thus ${\cal P}_0$ is a non empty set and has at least one infinite chain. Partial order property follows easily. If $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ and $\pi_2 \prec \pi_3$ then $\pi_1 \prec \pi_3$. 
If $U_{12}$ and $U_{23}$ are isometric operators that satisfies (C1)-(C3) respectively, then $U_{13}=U_{23}U_{12}$ will do the job for $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$. 
 
\vskip 1em 
However by Hausdorff maximality theorem there exists a non-empty maximal totally ordered subset ${\cal P}_0$ of ${\cal P}$. We claim that 
$\pi_{max}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} \pi$ on $H_{\pi_{max}}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} H_{\pi} $ is an upper bound 
in ${\cal P}_0$. That $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}$ is obvious. Further given an element $(H_1,\pi_1,\Omega_1) \in {\cal P}_0$ there exists 
an element $(H_2,\pi_2,\Omega_2) \in {\cal P}_0$ so that $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ by our starting remark as $\pi_0 \prec \pi_u$. 
By extending isometry $U_{12}$ to an isometry from $H_1 \rightarrow n_{\pi_{max}} H_{\pi_{max}}$ trivially we get the 
required isometry that satisfies (C1),(C2) and (C3) where cardinal numbers $n_{\pi_{max}} = \sum_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} 
n_{\pi} \in \aleph_0$. Thus by maximal property of ${\cal P}_0$ we have $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}_0$. This brings a contradiction 
as by our construction $(\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega) \prec (\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega)$ 
as $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}_0$ but partial order is strict. This contradicts our starting hypothesis that $\tilde{{\cal M}}$ is 
a proper subset of ${\cal M}'$. This completes the proof for (i) of (e) ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$ when $P=Q$.  

\vskip 1em 
In the proof of ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$ in (e), we have used equality $P=Q$ just to ensure that $\Omega$ is also a cyclic for $\tilde{{\cal M}}$ and $P=Q$ is used 
to prove $\pi({\cal O}_d)' = \pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''$. So (f) follows by the proof of (e). 

\vskip 1em 
A proof for (g) is given in [Mo3] with ${\cal M}_0$. Here we will also give an alternative proof relating the criteria obtained in Proposition 3.4. 
To that end we claim that $$\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)')=\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'
\bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'.$$ That $\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)') \subseteq \{ \tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J: |I|=|J| < \infty \}'$ follows by 
Cuntz relation and thus $\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)') \subseteq \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap 
\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'$. For the reverse inclusion let $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'$. For $n \ge 1$, 
we choose $|I|=n$ and set $Y_n=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I$. 
We check that it is independent of the index that we have chosen as 
$Y_n=\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J\tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_I\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_JX \tilde{S}_J=\tilde{S}^*_JX\tilde{S}_J$ 
where in second equality we have used $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ and also 
$\Lambda^n(Y_n)=\sum_{|J|=n } \tilde{S}_J\tilde{S}^*_IX\tilde{S}_I\tilde{S}^*_J=X$. This proves the equality in the claim. Going along the same line we also get 
$$\bigcap_{n \ge 1}\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi({\cal O}_d)') = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'\bigcap \pi({\cal O}_d)'= \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d)'.$$ 

\vskip 1em 
By Proposition 3.4 $\omega$ is pure if and only if the set above is trivial. Thus once more by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] and 
Theorem 2.4 in [Mo2], purity is equivalent to asymptotic relation $||\psi \tilde{\tau}^n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ 
for any normal state $\psi$ on ${\cal M}'$ ( Here we recall by Proposition 2.4 
$P\pi({\cal O}_d)'P={\cal M}'$ as $P$ is also the support projection 
in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''{\cal F}$ and support projection of $\phi_{\Omega}$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ 
is ${\cal F}=[\pi({\cal O}_d)''\Omega]$, where commutant is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$ ). 
By a duality argument Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3] we conclude that $\omega$ is pure if and only if there exists 
a sequence of elements $x_n \in {\cal M}$ so that for each $m \ge 0$, $x_{m+n}\tau_n(x) \rightarrow \phi(x)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $x \in {\cal M} \subseteq {\cal B}({\cal K})$. 
This completes the proof of (d) with ${\cal M}$. For the proof with ${\cal M}_0$ we need to show if part as only if part follows ${\cal M}_0$ being a subset of ${\cal M}$ and $\tau$ 
takes elements of ${\cal M}_0$ to itself. For if part we refer to Theorem 3.2 in [Mo3].

proof.raw:
First we will prove that $\omega$ is pure if $P$ is also the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$, 
where $\tilde{{\cal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\Omega]$. The support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is $\tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ and thus we also 
have $P = \tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ by our hypothesis. Since $\Lambda^n(P)=\Lambda^n({\cal E}){\cal F} \uparrow {\cal F}$ and now
$\Lambda^n(P)=\tilde{{\cal E}}\Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \uparrow \tilde{{\cal E}}$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, we also have 
${\cal F} = \tilde{{\cal E}}$. Similarly we also have for each $n$, ${\cal E}\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\cal E}})\tilde{{\cal F}}$ 
and thus taking limit we also get ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$.  

\vskip 1em 
So we have $P={\cal E} {\cal F}={\cal E} \tilde{{\cal E}}=Q$. $\tilde{{\cal M}}=P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P$ is cyclic in ${\cal K}$ i.e. 
$[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=[P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P\Omega]= P\tilde{{\cal F}}=P{\cal E}=P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$.  

\vskip 1em 
However $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)) = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ ( for a proof which is a simple 
application of Cuntz relation, we refer to section 5 of [Mo2]). Further $\psi$ being a factor state in $K_{\omega'}$, by Proposition 3.2 $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is a factor. 
In particular we have $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d))\tilde{{\cal F}} = \mathbb{C} \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Thus by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] we conclude that $||\Psi \circ \tilde{\tau}_n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ 
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all normal state $\Psi$ on $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=P \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ and support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ 
is $\tilde{{\cal E}}$ and $P={\cal E}\tilde{{\cal E}}{\cal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
Note that $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0 \subseteq {\cal M}_0'$ where ${\cal M}_0=P\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''P$. Further by Proposition 2.5 
${\cal M}_0 = \{x \in {\cal M}:\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}\;\;\;$ and  $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=\{x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}:
\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}$. Once we set $P_0=[{\cal M}_0\Omega]$ then we also have $P_0=[\tilde{{\cal M}}_0\Omega]$ 
as $[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=P=[{\cal M}\Omega]$ by expending $u_z=\sum_{k \in \hat{H}} z^kP_k$ where $z \rightarrow u_z=
PU_zP$ is a unitary representation of group $H$.      

\vskip 1em
For $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}, y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$ we have  
$$\phi(\tilde{\tau}(x)y)=\sum_k <\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega,x\tilde{v}^*_ky\Omega> = \sum_k <v^*_k\Omega,x y \tilde{v}^*_k\Omega>$$  
(as $v_k^*\Omega=\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega$ )
$$=\sum_k <\Omega, x v_kyv_k^* \Omega>=\phi(x \tau(y))$$
The dual group of $(\tilde{{\cal M}},\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given on the commutant by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}',\tau,\phi)$ where $\tau(x)=\sum_k v_k x v_k^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$. 
where commutant is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$. 
Now moving to $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in the duality relation above, we verify that 
adjoint Markov map of $(\tilde{{\cal M}}_0,\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0,\tau,\phi)$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$, the commutant of $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ 
is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$ and ${\cal K}_0$ is the Hilbert subspace $P_0$ with $\Omega$ as
cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ in ${\cal K}_0$. Thus by Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3], 
there exists a sequence of elements $y_n \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$ such that for each $m \ge 1$, 
$y_{m+n}\tau_n(y) \rightarrow \phi(y)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0 \subseteq {\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$. 
Thus $\omega$ is pure by Proposition 3.5 (e) once we recall ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$ as $P=Q$ 
( and so ${\cal M}'_0 = \tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ ) by Proposition 3.5 (d). This completes the proof of
 purity property of $\omega$. 


\vskip 1em  
In the following we now prove the hardest part of the theorem namely $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ and ${\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}$ if $\omega$ is pure. Proof uses extensively 
the general theory of quasi-equivalent representation of a $C^*$ algebra and we refer [BR1, Chapter 2.4.4] as a general reference.   

\vskip 1em 
We set unitary operator $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}^*_k$. That $V$ is a unitary operator follows by Cuntz's relations and commuting property 
of $(S_i)$ and $(\tilde{S}_i)$. Further a simple computation shows that $V\pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\cal B} = {\cal B}_L \otimes {\cal B}_R$, 
identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ and $\theta$ is the right shift. We also have    
\begin{equation} 
\theta({\cal E})=V {\cal E} V^*= \sum_{k,k'}S_k\tilde{S}^*_k {\cal E} S^*_{k'}\tilde{S}_{k'}=\Lambda({\cal E}) \ge {\cal E}
\end{equation} 
Similarly we also have
\begin{equation} 
\theta(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}} 
\end{equation}
So in particular we have $V(I-{\cal E})V^* \le I-{\cal E}$, i.e. $(I-{\cal E})V^*{\cal E}=0$.  
Also for any $X \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$ we have $V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}X\Omega = 
\tilde{{\cal F}} \sum_k \tilde{S}_k X \tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$ as $S_k^*\Omega 
=\tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$. Thus $(I-\tilde{{\cal F}})V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}=0$ i.e. 
$V\tilde{{\cal F}}V^*=\Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Similarly we also 
have 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\cal E}})=V^*\tilde{{\cal E}}V \ge \tilde{{\cal E}}\;\mbox{and}\; V^* {\cal F} V \ge {\cal F}
\end{equation} 
We also set two family of increasing projections for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ as follows 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal E}_n=V^n {\cal E} (V^n)^*,\;\;\tilde{{\cal F}}_n=V^n\tilde{{\cal F}}(V^n)^*
\end{equation}

\vskip 1em 
Since $\beta_z(V)=V$ for all $z \in H$, $V \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by Proposition 3.4 as $\omega$ is pure. $\omega$ being also a factor state, we have $<f,V^ng> \rightarrow <f,\Omega><\Omega,g>$ as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$ for any $f,g \in \pi({\cal B}_{loc})\Omega$ by Power's criteria [Pow] given in (1). Since such vectors are dense in the Hilbert space topology and the family $\{V^n:n \ge 1\}$ is uniformly bounded, we get $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$.   

\vskip 1em 
For the time being we assume that $H$ is trivial. Otherwise the argument that follows here we can use for the representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ i.e. $\pi$ restricted to $[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. 

\vskip 1em 
We have following distinct cases: 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 1.} ${\cal E} \neq I \;( \tilde{{\cal E}} \neq I)$. Let ${\cal E}_n \rightarrow {\cal E}_{-\infty}$ as $n \rightarrow -\infty$ and thus $V{\cal E}_{-\infty}V^*={\cal E}_{-\infty}$. We claim that either ${\cal E}_{-\infty} = |\Omega><\Omega|$ or ${\cal E}_{-\infty}$ is a proper infinite dimensional projection i.e. if ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ is a finite projection then ${\cal E}_{- \infty}=|\Omega><\Omega|$. Suppose not then the finite subspace is shift invariant. In particular there exists a unit  vector $f$ orthogonal to $\Omega$ such that $Vf=zf$ for some $z \in S^1$ and this contradicts weak mixing property i.e. $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology proved above as point spectrum of $V$ has only $1$ with spectral multiplicity $1$. 

\vskip 1em 
If ${\cal E}_{-\infty}$ is infinite dimensional we can get a unitary operator $U_0$ from 
$F_0=\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H}$ onto ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ and 
via the unitary map we can get a sequence of increasing projections $U_0{\cal E}_nU^*_0$ in ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ and note that $U_0{\cal E}_nU_0^*=V^nU_0 {\cal E} U_0^*(V^n)^*$. Note that if ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ is infinite dimension the process will not stop in finite step. Thus we have $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{{\cal E}}} F(k)$ where the index set is either singleton or infinity and each $F(k)$ will give a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$, where $F(1)
=F_0-{\cal E}_{-\infty}$. Further $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ being a simple $C^*$-algebra, each such imprimitivity system 
is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ [Mo3,section 4]: We fix a nonzero $f \in {\cal E}-\theta^{-1}({\cal E}) \neq 0$ otherwise ${\cal E}=I$ as $\theta^n({\cal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. $\pi_f:x \rightarrow \theta^{-1}(x)f$ gives a representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d={\cal B}_L$ and we check that $[\pi_f(\theta^{-1}({\cal B}_L)''f] \le {\cal E}-\theta^{-1}({\cal E})$ 
as $f \perp [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\cal B}_R)')\Omega] \ge [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\cal B}_L))\Omega]$. Thus simplicity 
ensures that ${\cal E} - \theta^{-1}({\cal E})$ is a projection of dimension $\aleph_0$. Further $n_{\cal E}$ is either $1$
or $\aleph_0$ since $F_0$ is separable.   

\vskip 1em 
Since $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is also a proper projection, same argument is valid for $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ with $\tilde{{\cal F}}_{-\infty}=
\mbox{lim}_{n \rightarrow -\infty} \theta^n(\tilde{{\cal F}})$ i.e. we can write $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{\tilde{{\cal F}}}} \tilde{H}(k)$, where each $\tilde{H}(k)$ give rises to a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$ where each system of imprimitivity is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ where $\tilde{F}(1) = F_0-\tilde{{\cal F}}_{-\infty}$ 
and $n_{\tilde{{\cal F}}}$ is either $1$ or $\aleph_0$.        

\vskip 1em 
In the following we use temporary notation $H$ for Hilbert subspace $F_0$. For a cardinal number $n$, we 
amplify a representation $\pi:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(H)$ of the $C^*$ algebra ${\cal B}$ to $n$ fold direct sum 
$n\pi=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } \pi_k $ acting on $nH=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } H_k$  defining by 
$$n\pi(x) (\oplus \zeta_k) = \oplus (\pi(x)\zeta_k)$$ 
where $\pi_k = \pi$ is the representation of ${\cal B}=\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ 
on $H_k=H$ where $H =[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. We also 
extend $\bar{\tilde{F}} = \oplus \tilde{F}_{\alpha}$, $\bar{E} = \oplus E_{\alpha}$ and $\bar{V}=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n} V_k$ respectively. We also set notation $\Omega_k=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}\delta^k_j\Omega$. 

\vskip 1em 
Thus by Mackey's theorem, there exists a cardinal number $n \in \aleph_0$ and a unitary operator $U: nH \rightarrow nH$ so that 
$\bar{V}=U\bar{V}U^*$ and $\bar{{\cal E}}=U\bar{\tilde{{\cal F}}}U^*$. We set a representation 
$\pi^U:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(nH)$ by $\pi^U(x)= Un\pi(x)U^*$
and rewrite the above identity as 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^U_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$
where $\pi^U_k(x)=U\pi_k(x)U^*$. Note that by our construction we 
can ensure $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ for all $1 \le k \le n$ as the operator 
intertwining between two imprimitivity systems are acting on the orthogonal 
subspace of the projection generated by vectors $\{\Omega_k:1 \le k \le n\}$. 

\vskip 1em 
We claim ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}$. In such a case we 
have
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k]$$
Alternatively 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$

\vskip 1em 
Thus in principle we can repeat our construction now with $\pi^U$ and so we 
get a strict partial ordered set of quasi-equivalent representation of ${\cal B}$. 
In the following we now aim to employ formal set theory to bring a contradiction 
on our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
To that end we need to deal with more then one representation of ${\cal B}$. For the rest of the proof we reset notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ used for the pure representation of 
${\cal B}$ in $H_0 =[\pi_0({\cal B})\Omega_0]$ where $\Omega_0$ is the cyclic vector, the reset notation for $\Omega$. Let ${\cal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ 
quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(H_0)$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. $\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists 
minimal cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus for such an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega_{\pi})$ we can associate

with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ if there exists an 
isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that

\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have

$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;
