\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 2:} ${\cal E}=I \;(\tilde{{\cal E}}=I)$. We need to show $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I\;({\cal F}=I)$ respectively. Suppose not and assume that both $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is a proper non-zero projection. 

\vskip 1em 
We set projection $G$ on the closed linear span of elements in the subspaces $[\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]$ for all $n \ge 0$. We recall that $\theta(X)=VXV^*$ 
where $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}_k^*$ and $\theta^{-1}(X)=\tilde{\Lambda}(X)$ 
for $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. Thus we have 
$$V^*\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\cal F})V^*\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''V\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\cal F}) \tilde{\Lambda}(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega.$$
Thus $(1-G)V^*G=0$ i.e. $\theta(G) \ge G$. It is also clear that $\tilde{{\cal F}} \le G$ 
as the defining sequence of subspaces of $G$ goes to precisely $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ ( recall 
that $\theta^{-n}({\cal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}_n({\cal F}) \uparrow I$ strongly as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). Once more we have 
$\theta^n(G) \ge \theta^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow 
\infty$.  

\vskip 1em 
If $G$ is a proper projection we can follow the steps as in the case 1 to find a unitary operator 
$U:nH \rightarrow nH$ with $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ and $U\bar{V}U^*=\bar{V}$ so that $U\bar{G}U^*=\bar{\tilde{{\cal F}}}$. 
We consider the subset ${\cal P}_G$ of elements in ${\cal P}$ for which ${\cal E}_{\pi}=1$ and 
$\{\theta^{-n}({\cal F}_{\pi}):n \ge 0 \}$ commutes with $\tilde{{\cal F}}_{\pi}$ 
and modify the strict partial ordering by modifying (C3) as  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] <  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\noindent So we also get $\pi^U \in {\cal P}_G$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$ and going along the same line we conclude that 
$G=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. Thus we conclude that $G$ is either equal to $1$ or $G=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 1 of case 2:} If $G=I$ then ${\cal F} G = {\cal F}$ and so $[{\cal F}\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]={\cal F}$ as $\theta^{-n}({\cal F}) \ge {\cal F}$. 
Thus $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge {\cal F}$. So $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge \tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F})$ for all $n \ge 1$ and taking limit we get $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge I$ i.e. $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I$. 
This contradicts our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is a proper projection.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 2 of case 2:} Now we consider the case $G=\tilde{{\cal F}} < I$. In such a case we have 
$(1- \tilde{{\cal F}})\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\tilde{{\cal F}}=0$ and so $\theta^{-n}({\cal F})$ commutes with $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ for all $n \ge 0$. 

\vskip 1em 
First we rule out the simplest possibility in the present situation for ${\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} = |\Omega><\Omega|$. If so then $\omega$ is
a Bernoulli state and a proof follows once we compute the following using the property $\Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$ i.e.
$\tilde{{\cal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}$ 
and commuting property of ${\cal F}$ with $\pi(s_i)^*$ to get some scalars $\bar{\lambda_i}$ such
that 
$$\bar{\lambda}_i= {\cal F}\tilde{{\cal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F}$$
and so 
$$\omega(s_Is_J^*)=<\Omega,\pi(s_I) \pi(s_J)^*\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega, {\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} \pi(s_I)\pi(s_J)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F} \Omega>$$
$$=\lambda_I\lambda_J^*$$
The inductive limit state $\omega$ on ${\cal B}$, give rises to a pure state once restricted to ${\cal B}_R$ and thus we have 
${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$ by Haag duality when $\pi({\cal B}_R)''$ is a type-I factor. This contradicts our starting assumption that ${\cal E}=I$.   

\vskip 1em 
Now we set projection ${\cal F}'$ defined by 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal F}'={\cal F}-{\cal F}\tilde{{\cal F}}+|\Omega><\Omega|
\end{equation} 
and check by commuting property of $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ with ${\cal F}$ that 
$$ 
{\cal F}'\theta^{-1}({\cal F}'){\cal F}' = (I-\tilde{{\cal F}}){\cal F}\theta^{-1}({\cal F})(I-\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\cal F}}))(I-\tilde{{\cal F}}){\cal F} 
+ |\Omega><\Omega|$$ 
$$= {\cal F}(I-\tilde{{\cal F}}) + |\Omega><\Omega|={\cal F}'$$ 
where we have used $\theta^{-1}({\cal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}({\cal F}) \ge {\cal F},\; \theta({\cal F}) \le {\cal F}$ and  
$\theta(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$. 
Thus we get 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}({\cal F}') \ge {\cal F}'
\end{equation}                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     

\vskip 1em 
We also rule out the possibility that ${\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} = {\cal F}$. If so then ${\cal F} \le \tilde{{\cal F}}$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F}) \le 
\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Taking limit we get $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I$ as $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. 
This brings a contradiction to our hypothesis.  
  
\vskip 1em 
So we have in particular ${\cal F}' <  {\cal F} \le I$ and ${\cal F}' - |\Omega><\Omega| \neq 0$. Now we will rule out the possibility of ${\cal F}=I$ under our hypothesis $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}=I$.

Now we consider a further subset ${\cal P}_{G'}$ of ${\cal P}_G$ consist of quasi-equivalent representations $\pi$ to $\pi_0$

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3'') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] >  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

Since $\pi^U$ also satisfies the conditions that of $\pi_0 \in {\cal P}_{G'}$ by covariance relation 
of $U$ with respect to shifts once more we get $\pi^U \in {\cal P}_{G'}$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus we can 
repeat the process and so ${\cal P}_{G'}$ has at least one infinite chain of totally ordered containing $\pi_0$.   
Once more by Hausdorff maximality principle we bring a contradiction to our starting assumption 
that ${\cal F}' < {\cal F}$. In other words this brings a contradiction to our starting hypothesis 
that $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is a proper projection i.e. ${\cal F} < {\cal E}=I$. Thus we arrive at $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ 
when ${\cal E}=I$. 

\vskip 1em 
By symmetry of argument used here it also follows that ${\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\cal E}}=I$. This completes the proof of 
$\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E},\;\; {\cal F} =\tilde{{\cal E}}$ for the case when $H$ is the trivial closed subgroup of $S^1$.

By applying the first part of the argument with representation $\pi_0$, for pure $\omega$, we have 
$e_0=\tilde{f}_0$ and $\tilde{e}_0=f_0$ and $p_0=q_0$.

If $H=\{z:z^n=1 \}$ then we get $P=\sum_k PF_k=\sum_k QF_k=Q$. This completes the proof for $P=Q$. Similarly

If $H=S^1$ then $\hat{H}=\mathbb{Z}$ and for $m \ge 0$, we have $PF_m=QF_m$. For $m < 0$ we take $k=-m$ and

Thus so far we have taken an arbitrary element $\psi \in K_{\omega}$ and worked with its support projection to arrive at a representation of $\omega$ given in (7) or (8) by Popescu's elements 
${\cal P}=\{({\cal K},v_i \in {\cal M},1 \le i \le d\;\Omega): \sum_kv_iv_i^*=I \}$. However by Lemma 7.4 in [BJKW] for a factor state $\omega$, if we choose an extreme point $\psi \in K_{\omega}$, 
two such extreme points $\psi$ and $\psi'$ in $K_{\omega}$ are related by $\psi'=\phi \beta_z$ for some $z \in S^1$, ${\cal P}$ is uniquely determined modulo a unitary conjugation. In other words we find a 
one-one correspondence between 
\begin{equation}
\omega \Leftrightarrow \omega_R \Leftrightarrow K^e_{\omega} \Leftrightarrow {\cal P}_e 
\end{equation}  
modulo unitary conjugation where $K^e_{\omega}$ denotes the set of extreme points in $K_{\omega}$ and ${\cal P}_e$ the set of Popescu's elements associated with extreme points 
of $K_{\omega}$ on support projection of the state as described above. Further in such a case ${\cal M}=\{v_k:1 \le k \le d\}''$ 
is a factor and $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is an ergodic {\it quantum dynamical system } [La,Ev]. A unital completely positive map $\tau$ on a von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}$ 
with an invariant normal state $\phi$ [BJKW,Mo1] is called {\it ergodic} if 
\begin{equation} 
{1 \over N}\sum_{0 \le k \le N-1}\tau^k(x) \rightarrow  \phi(x)I
\end{equation} 
as $N \rightarrow \infty$ in weak$^*$ topology for all $x \in {\cal M}$. Thus any symmetry of $\omega$ will act on Popescu elements ${\cal P}_e$ via this correspondence. It would be worthwhile 
to have a result generalizing this correspondence in a more general situation that Ruy Exel developed [Ex].

\vskip 1em 
Before we elaborate further on equivalence of above statements we briefly recall results on translation invariant pure state on ${\cal B} =\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}M_d(\mathbb{C})$ that finds its relevance while proving Haag duality property. There is a one to one affine map between translation invariant states on ${\cal B}$ and translation invariant states on ${\cal B}_R =\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_+}M_d(\mathbb{C})$ by $\omega \rightarrow \omega_R=\omega_{|{\cal B}_R}$. The inverse map is the inductive limit 
state of $({\cal B}_R,\psi_R) \rightarrow^{\lambda_n} ({\cal B}_R,\psi_R)$ where $(\lambda_n:n \ge 0)$ is the canonical semi-group of right shifts on ${\cal B}_R$. Pure states on a $\mbox{UHF}$ algebra are studied in the general framework of [Pow]. Such a situation has been investigated also in detail at various degrees of generality in [BJP] and [BJKW] motivated by the development a $C^*$ algebraic method in the study of iterative function systems and its associated wavelet theory. One interesting result in [BJP] says that any translation invariant pure state on ${\cal B}_R$ is also a product state and the canonical endomorphism associated with two such states are unitary equivalent. However such a statement is not true for two translation invariant pure states on ${\cal B}$ as their restriction to ${\cal B}_R$ need not be isomorphic. Theorem 3.4 in [Mo4] says that $\omega_R$ is either a type-I or a type-III factor state on ${\cal B}_R$. Both type of factors are known to exist in the literature of quantum statistical mechanics [BR vol-II,Si,Ma1]. Thus the classification problem of translation dynamics on ${\cal B}$ with invariant pure states on ${\cal B}$ up to unitary isomorphism is a delicate one. In this context one interesting problem that remain open is whether mean entropy [Ru] is an invariance for translation dynamics.   

\vskip 1em 
Since a $\theta$ invariant state $\omega$ on ${\cal B}$ is completely determined by its restriction $\omega_R$ to ${\cal B}_R$, in principle it is possible to describe various properties of $\omega$ including purity by studying their restriction $\omega_R$. 
Theorem 3.2 in [Mo3] gives a precise answer: $\omega$ is pure if and only if there exists a sequence of positive contractive elements $x_n \in {\cal M}$ such that 
$$x_n \rightarrow I,\;\;x_{m+n}\tau_n(x) \rightarrow \phi(x)I$$ 
in strong operator topology for all $x \in {\cal M}$ and $m \ge 1$. As an application of this result, we prove that (e) implies (f). 
This statement can be taken as the correct version of Theorem 7.1 of [BJKW]. Theorem 7.1 in [BJKW] has aimed towards a sufficient condition on Popescu elements ${\cal P}$ for purity of the translation invariant state. However the statement and its proof are faulty as certain argument used in the proof is not time reversal symmetric and a factor state with Popescu elements on support projection satisfies the conditions of the statement of Theorem 7.1. One natural remedy to add additional hypothesis that (e) holds. In particular Lemma 7.6 in [BJKW] needs that additional assumption related to the support projection of the dual state $\tilde{\psi} \in K_{\tilde{\omega}}$. Besides this additional structure proof of Lemma 7.8 in [BJKW] is also not complete unless we find a proof for $\tilde{{\cal M}}={\cal M}'$ ( we retained same notations here in the text) for such a factor state $\omega$. Such a problem could have been solved if there were any method which shows directly that Takesaki's conditional [Ta] expectation exists from ${\cal M}'$ onto $\tilde{{\cal M}}$. For von-Neumann algebras ${\cal N} \subseteq {\cal M}$, a normal unital completely positive map $E_c:{\cal M} \rightarrow {\cal N}$ is called 
{\it normal conditional expectation } if 
\begin{equation} 
E_c(yxz)=yE_c(x)z
\end{equation}
for all $y,z \in {\cal N}$ and $x \in {\cal M}$. 
A theorem of Takesaki's [Ta, also see AcC] says that conditional expectation $E_c$ preserving a faithful normal state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ exists if and only if the modular group $\sigma=(\sigma_t:t \in \mathbb{R})$ 
associated with $\phi$, which preserves ${\cal M}$, also preserves ${\cal N}$, i.e. $\sigma_t(x) \in {\cal N}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in {\cal N}$. Thus main body of the proof for Theorem 7.1 even with the 
additional natural hypothesis $p_0=q_0$, in [BJKW] is incomplete. 

\vskip 1em 
Besides the proof of (e) implies (f), other implication follows along with while we will prove the hardest part of this theorem namely (f) implies (c) i.e. purity implies Haag duality property (16). For the proof 
we have explored the set of representation of ${\cal B}$ quasi-equivalent to $\pi_{\omega}$ and equip it with a strict partial ordering depending on our situation to prove Haag duality. Mackey's system of imprimitivity [Mac] 
plays a crucial role even though a pure state not necessarily give rise to a Mackey's system of imprimitivity generated by the support projection $e_0$ with respect to shift. Though we have worked here with amalgamated representation 
of $\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d$ in [BJKW], it seems that just for Haag duality one can avoid doing so. It seems that the underlining group $\mathbb{Z}$ can easily be replaced by $\mathbb{Z}^k$ for some $k \ge 2$ and 
wedge duality for a pointed cone can be proved by following the same ideas. We defer this line of analysis leaving it for work as its relation with problems in quantum spin 
chain in higher dimensional lattice needs some additional structure. We also defer application of Haag duality property in studying symmetry and correlation of a translation invariant pure state to another
paper [Mo5].  

\vskip 1em
The paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we study Popescu's dilation associated with a translation invariant state on Cuntz algebra ${\cal O}_d$ and review `commutant lifting theorem' investigated in [BJKW]. 
The proof presented here remove the murky part of the proof of Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. In section 3 we explore both the notion of Kolmogorov's shift and its intimate relation with Mackey's imprimitivity system 
to explore a duality argument introduced in [BJKW]. We find a useful necessary and sufficient condition (Theorem 1.1 (a) ) in terms of support projection of Cuntz's state for a translation invariant factor state 
$\omega$ on ${\cal B}$ to be pure. The criterion on support projection is crucial for our main mathematical result Theorem 3.6. 

\begin{rem} 
The paper ``On Haag Duality for Pure States of Quantum Spin Chain'' 
by authors: M. Keyl, Taku Matsui, D. Schlingemann, R. F. Werner, Rev. Math. Phys. 20:707-724,2008 has an incomplete proof for Haag duality property as Lemma 4.3 in that paper has a faulty argument.   
\end{rem}

\vskip 1em
\begin{proof}
Following Popescu [Po] we define a completely positive map
$R: {\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$ by
\begin{equation}
R(s_Is^*_J)=v_Iv^*_J
\end{equation}
for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$. The representation $S_1,..,S_d$ of ${\cal O}_d$ on ${\cal H}$ thus may be taken to be the Stinespring
dilation of $R$ [BR, vol-2] and uniqueness up to unitary equivalence follows from uniqueness of the Stinespring
representation. That ${\cal K}$ is cyclic for the representation follows from the minimality property of the Stinespring
dilation. 

\vskip 1em 
For (a) let $Q$ be the limiting projection of $\Lambda^n(P)$ as $n \uparrow \infty$. Then we have $\Lambda(Q)=Q$ i.e. $Q\Lambda(I-Q)Q=0$ 
and so $(I-Q)S_k^*Q=0$. Interchanging the role of $Q$ with $I-Q$, we get $QS_k^*(I-Q)=0$. This shows $QS_k^*=S_k^*Q$ for all $1 le k \le d$. 
Since $Q$ is a projection, taking adjoint in the relation, we get $Q \in \{S_k,S^*_k\}'$. That $Q \ge P$ is obvious since $\Lambda^n(P) \ge P$ 
for all $n \ge 1$. In particular $QS_If=S_If$ for all $f \in {\cal K}$ and $|I| < \infty$. Hence $Q=I$ by the
cyclicity of ${\cal K}$. 

\vskip 1em 
For (b) essentially we deffer from the argument used in Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. We fix any $D
\in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ and note that $P\Lambda_k(D)P=\tau_k(D)=D$ for any $k \ge 1$. Thus for any integers $n > m$
we have
$$\Lambda_m(P)\Lambda_n(D)\Lambda_m(P)=\Lambda_m(P\Lambda_{n-m}(D)P)=\Lambda_m(D)$$
Hence for any fixed $m \ge 1$ limit $<f,\Lambda_n(D)g>$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ exists for all
$f,g \in \Lambda_m(P)$. Since the family of operators $\Lambda_n(D)$ is uniformly bounded and $\Lambda_m(P) \uparrow I$
as $m \rightarrow \infty$, a standard density argument guarantees that the weak operator limit of $\Lambda_n(D)$ exists as
$n \rightarrow \infty$. Let $X'$ be the limit. So $\Lambda(X')=X'$, by Cuntz's relation, $X' \in \{S_k,S^*_k:1 \le k \le k \}'$.
Since $P\Lambda_n(D)P=D$ for all $n \ge 1$, we also conclude that $PX'P=D$ by taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$. Conversely,
it is obvious that $P\{ S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P \subseteq {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$. Hence
we can identify $P\{S_k,S^*_k:\; k \ge 1 \}'P$ with ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Further it is obvious that $X'$ is self-adjoint if and only if $D=PX'P$ is self-adjoint ( since $\Lambda^n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, 
by taking limit $\Lambda^n(PXP)=\Lambda^n(PX^*P)$ shows that $X^*=X$ if $D^*=D$ ). Now fix any self-adjoint element $D \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$. Since 
the identity operator on ${\cal K}$ is an element in ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ for any $\alpha \ge 0$ for which $- \alpha P  \le D \le \alpha P$, we have $\alpha 
\Lambda_n(P) \le \Lambda_n(D) \le \alpha \Lambda_n(P)$ for all $n \ge 1$. By taking limit $n \rightarrow \infty$ we
conclude that $- \alpha I \le X' \le \alpha I$, where $PX'P=D$. Since operator norm of a self-adjoint element $A$
in a Hilbert space is given by
$$||A||= \mbox{inf}_{\alpha \ge 0}\{\alpha: - \alpha I  \le A \le \alpha I \}$$
we conclude that $||X'|| \le ||D||$. That $||D||=||PX'P|| \le ||X'||$ is obvious, $P$ being a
projection. Thus the map is isometrically order isomorphic taking self-adjoint elements of the commutant
to self-adjoint elements of ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
We are left to prove (c). Inclusion is trivial. For the last part, we assume first that $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$. For any element $D$
in ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d\}'$ so that $PX'P=D$. Since $P$ commutes with $X'$, 
we verify that 
$$Dv^*_k= PX'PS^*_kP=PX'S^*_kP=PS^*_kX'P=PS^*_kPX'P=v^*_kD$$ 
We also have $D^* \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ and thus $D^*v^*_k=v^*_kD^*$. Hence $D \in \{v_k,v^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'$. Since $P\pi_{\hat{\omega}}
({\cal O}_d)'P = {\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau}$, we conclude that ${\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M}'$. Thus equality holds whenever
$P \in \{S_k,S_k^*,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$. 

\vskip 1em 
For the converse note that by commutant lifting property self-adjoint elements
of the commutant $\{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}'$ is order isometric with the algebra ${\cal M}'$ via the map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$.
Hence $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}''$ by Proposition 4.2 in [BJKW]. 

\vskip 1em 
For the proof of intertwining relation and their property we refer to main body of the proof of 
Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. 
\end{proof}

\vskip 1em
A family $(v_k,1 \le k \le d)$ of contractive operators on a Hilbert space ${\cal K}$ is called Popescu's elements if $\sum_kv_kv_k^*=I$ 
and the dilation $({\cal H},P,{\cal K},S_k,1 \le k \le d)$ in Theorem 2.1 is called Popescu's dilation to Cuntz elements. In the 
following proposition we deal with a family of minimal Popescu elements for a state on ${\cal O}_d$. 

\begin{pro}
There exists a canonical one-one correspondence between the following objects:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) States $\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) Function $C: {\cal I} \times {\cal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with the following properties:

\noindent (i) $C(\emptyset, \emptyset)=1$;

\noindent (ii) for any function $\lambda:{\cal I} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with finite support we have
         $$\sum_{I,J \in {\cal I}} \overline{\lambda(I)}C(I,J)\lambda(J) \ge 0$$

\noindent (iii) $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_d} C(Ii,Ji) = C(I,J)$ for all $I,J \in {\cal I}$.

\vskip 1em
\noindent (c) Unitary equivalence class of objects $({\cal K},\Omega,v_1,..,v_d)$ where

\noindent (i) ${\cal K}$ is a Hilbert space and $\Omega$ is a unit vector in ${\cal K}$;

\noindent (ii) $v_1,..,v_d \in {\cal B}({\cal K})$ so that $\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_d} v_iv^*_i=1$;

\noindent (iii) the linear span of the vectors of the form $v^*_I\Omega$, where $I \in {\cal I}$, is dense in ${\cal K}$.

\vskip 1em
The correspondence is given by a unique completely positive map $R: {\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$, where 

\noindent (i) $R(s_Is^*_J)=v_Iv^*_J;$

\noindent (ii) $\psi(x)=<\Omega,R(x)\Omega>;$

\noindent (iii) $\psi(s_Is^*_J)=C(I,J)=<v^*_I \Omega,v^*_J\Omega>;$

\noindent (iv) For any fixed $g \in U_d$, the completely positive map $R_g:{\cal O}_d \rightarrow {\cal B}({\cal K})$ defined by $R_g= R
\circ \beta_g$ give rises to a Popescu system given by $({\cal K},\Omega,\beta_g(v_i),..,\beta_g(v_d))$ where
$\beta_g(v_i)=\sum_{1 \le j \le d} \overline{g^i_j} v_j.$

\end{pro}

\vskip 1em
\begin{proof} 
For a proof we simply refer to Proposition 2.1 in [BJKW]. 
\end{proof} 

\vskip 1em
The following is a simple consequence of Theorem 2.1 valid for a $\lambda$-invariant state $\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$. 
This proposition will have very little application in the main body of this paper but this gives a clear picture explaining the
delicacy of the present problems. 

\begin{pro}

Let $\psi$ be a state on ${\cal O}_d$ and $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$ be the GNS space associated with 
$({\cal O}_d,\psi)$. We set $S_i=\pi(s_i)$ and normal state $\psi_{\Omega}$ on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ defined by 
$$\psi_{\Omega}(X) = <\Omega, X \Omega>$$
Let $P$ be the projection on the closed subspace ${\cal K}$ generated by the vectors $\{S^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ and 
\begin{equation}
v_k=PS_kP
\end{equation}
for $1 \le k \le d$. Then following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $\{v^*_I\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ is total in ${\cal K}$.

\noindent (b) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$;

\noindent (c) $S_k^*P=PS_k^*P$ for all $1 \le k \le d$; 

\noindent (d) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have 
\begin{equation} 
\psi(s_Is^*_J)= <\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>
\end{equation} 
and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\cal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in
the GNS Hilbert space associated with $({\cal O}_d,\psi)$. Further such a family $({\cal K},\;v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\;\omega)$ satisfying
(a) to (d) is determined uniquely up to isomorphism. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely given a Popescu system $({\cal K},v_k,\;1 \le k \le d,\Omega)$ satisfying (a) and (b) there exists a unique   state 
$\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ so that (c) and (d) are satisfied.

Furthermore the following statements are valid:
\vskip 1em
\noindent (e)  If the normal state $\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ on the von-Neumann algebra
${\cal M}=\{ v_i, v^*_i \}''$ is invariant for the Markov map $\tau(x)=\sum_{1 \le k
\le d} v_ixv^*_i,\;x \in {\cal M}$ then $\psi$ is $\lambda$ invariant and $\phi$ is faithful 
on ${\cal M}$.

\vskip 1em
\noindent (f) If $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ then following are equivalent:

\noindent (i) $\psi$ is an ergodic state for $({\cal O}_d,\lambda)$; 

\noindent (ii) $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) ${\cal M}$ is a factor. 
\end{pro} 

\vskip 1em
\begin{proof} 
We fix a state $\psi$ and consider the GNS space  $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$
associated with $({\cal O}_d,\psi)$ and set $S_i=\pi(s_i)$. It is obvious 
that $S^*_kP \subseteq P$ for all $1 \le k \le d $, thus $P$ is the minimal subspace 
containing $\Omega$ and invariant by all $\{ S^*_k;\;1 \le k \le d \}$ i.e.
\begin{equation}
PS^*_kP=S^*_kP
\end{equation}
Thus $v^*_k=PS^*_kP=S_k^*P$ and so $\sum_k v_kv^*_k = \sum_k PS_kS^*_kP= P$ which is 
identity operator in ${\cal K}$. This completes the proof of (a) (b) and (c).

\vskip 1em
For (d) we note that
$$\psi(s_Is^*_J)$$
$$=<\Omega, S_IS^*_J\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega,PS_IS^*_JP\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>.$$
Since ${\cal H}$ is spanned by the vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega:|I|,|J| < \infty \}$ and
${\cal K}$ is spanned by the vectors $\{ S^*_J\Omega=v^*_J\Omega:|I| < \infty \}$, 
${\cal K}$ is cyclic for $S_I$ i.e. the vectors $\{ S_I{\cal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ spans 
${\cal H}$. Uniqueness up to isomorphism follows as usual by total property of vectors 
$v^*_I\Omega$ in ${\cal K}$. 

\vskip 1em
Conversely for a Popescu's elements $({\cal K},v_i,\Omega)$ satisfying (a) and (b), we consider
the family $({\cal H},S_k,\;1 \le k \le d,P)$ of Cuntz's elements defined as in
Theorem 2.1. We claim that $\Omega$ is a cyclic vector for the representation $\pi(s_i) \rightarrow
S_i$. Note that by our construction vectors $\{S_If,f \in {\cal K}: |I| < \infty \}$ are total
in ${\cal H}$ and $v^*_J\Omega=S^*_J\Omega$ for all $|J| < \infty$. Thus by our hypothesis that
vectors $\{v^*_J\Omega:|I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal K}$, we verify that
vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega: |I|,|J| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal H}$. Hence $\Omega$ is a cyclic for
the representation $s_i \rightarrow S_i$ of ${\cal O}_d$.

\vskip 1em
We are left to prove (e) and (f). It simple to note by (d) that $\psi \lambda=\psi$ i.e.
$$\sum_i <\Omega,S_iS_IS^*_JS^*_i\Omega>= \sum_i <\Omega,v_iv_Iv^*_Jv^*_i\Omega> $$
$$=<\Omega,v_Iv_J^*\Omega> = <\Omega,S_IS^*_J\Omega>$$ for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$ where 
in the second equality we have used our hypothesis that the vector state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ 
is $\tau$-invariant. In such case we aim now to show that $\phi$ is faithful on ${\cal M}$. To that end 
let $p'$ be the support projection in ${\cal M}$ for $\tau$ invariant state $\phi$. Thus $\phi(1-p') = 0$ 
i.e. $p'\Omega=\Omega$ and by invariance we also have $\phi(p'\tau(1-p')p')=\phi(1-p')=0$. Since $p'\tau(1-p')p' \ge 0 $ and an element in 
${\cal M}$, by minimality of support projection, we 
conclude that $p'\tau(1-p')p'=0$. Hence $p'\Omega=\Omega$ and $p'v^*_kp'=v^*_kp'$ for all $1 \le k \le d$. 
Thus $p'v^*_I\Omega=v^*_I\Omega$ for all 
$|I| < \infty$. As ${\cal K}$ is the closed linear span of the vectors $\{ v_I^*\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$, we conclude 
that $p'=p$. In other words $\phi$ is faithful on ${\cal M}$. This completes the proof for (e).

\vskip 1em
We are left to show (f) where we assume that $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$. $\Omega$ being a cyclic vector for $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, the weak$^*$ limit of the increasing 
projection $\Lambda^k(P)$ is $I$. Thus by Theorem 3.6 in [Mo1] we have $(\pi({\cal O}_d)'',\Lambda,\psi_{\Omega})$ is ergodic if and only if the reduced dynamics 
$({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic. For the last part of the statement, we need to show for a projection $e \in {\cal M}$, $\tau(e)=e$ if and only if $e \in {\cal M} \bigcap {\cal M}'$.
It is an easy consequence since $\tau(e)=e$ says that $e\tau(I-e)e=0$ and so $(1-e)v_k^*e=0$. Changing the role of $e$ by $I-e$, we also get $ev_k^*(I-e)=0$ for
all $1 \le k \le d$. Thus we get that $e$ commutes with each $v_k$. $P$ being in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, $v_k \in {\cal M}$. So $e \in {\cal M}'$. Thus by a standard theorem [La,Ev,Fr,BJKW] 
ergodic property is equivalent to factor property of ${\cal M}$. 
\end{proof} 

\vskip 1em
Before we move to our next result, we comment here that in general for a $\lambda$ invariant state on ${\cal O}_d$, 
the normal state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}=\{v_k,v_k^*:1 \le k \le d \}''$ need not be invariant for $\tau$. To that 
end we consider ( [BR] vol-II page 110 ) the unique KMS state $\psi=\psi_{\beta}$ for the automorphism $\alpha_t(s_i)=e^{it}s_i$ on ${\cal O}_d$. $\psi$ is $\lambda$ 
invariant and $\psi_{|\mbox{UHF}_d}$ is the unique faithful trace. $\psi$ being a KMS state for an automorphism, the normal state induced by the cyclic vector on 
$\pi_{\psi}({\cal O}_d)''$ is also separating for $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. As $\psi \beta_z = \psi$ for all $z \in S^1$ we have 
$<\Omega,\pi(s_I)\Omega>=<\Omega,\beta_z(s_I)\Omega> = z^{|I|}<\Omega,\pi(s_I)\Omega>$ for all $z \in S^1$ and 
so $<\Omega,\pi(s_I)\Omega>=0$ for all $|I| \ge 1$. In particular $<\Omega,v_I^*\Omega>=0$ where $(v_i)$ are defined 
as in Proposition 2.3 and thus $<v_i\Omega,v^*_I\Omega>=<\Omega,v^*_iv_I\Omega>=0$ for all $1 \le i \le d$. Hence $v_i\Omega=0$. By Proposition 2.3 (e), $\Omega$ is 
separating for ${\cal M}$ and so we get $v_i=0$ for all $1 \le i \le d$ and this contradicts that $\sum_i v_iv_i^*=1$. Thus we conclude by Proposition 2.3 (e) that 
$\phi$ is not $\tau$ invariant on ${\cal M}$. This example also indicates that the support projection of a $\lambda$ invariant state $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ need 
not be equal to the minimal sub-harmonic projection $P$ i.e. the closed span of vectors $\{ S_I^*\Omega: |I| < \infty \}$ containing $\Omega$ and $\{v_Iv_J^*: |I|,|J| < \infty \}$ 
need not be even an algebra.        

\vskip 1em
Now we aim to deal with another class of Popescu elements associated with an $\lambda$-invariant state on ${\cal O}_d$. 
In fact this class of Popescu elements will play a significant role for the rest of the text and we will repeatedly use
this proposition in section 3. 

\vskip 1em
\begin{pro} 

Let $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$ be the GNS representation of a $\lambda$ invariant state 
$\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ and $P$ be the support projection of the normal state $\psi_{\Omega}(X)=<\Omega,X\Omega>$ in the 
von-Neumann algebra $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. Then the following holds:

\vskip 1em
\noindent (a) $P$ is a sub-harmonic projection for the endomorphism $\Lambda(X)=\sum_k S_kXS^*_k$ on $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$
i.e. $\Lambda(P) \ge P$ satisfying the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) $PS^*_kP=S^*_kP,\;\;1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (iii) $\sum_{1 \le k \le d} v_kv_k^*=I$ 

where $S_k=\pi(s_k)$ and $v_k=PS_kP$ for $1 \le k \le d$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (b) For any $I=(i_1,i_2,...,i_k),J=(j_1,j_2,...,j_l)$ with $|I|,|J| < \infty$ we have $\psi(s_Is^*_J) =
<\Omega,v_Iv^*_J\Omega>$ and the vectors $\{ S_If: f \in {\cal K},\;|I| < \infty \}$ are total in ${\cal H}$;

\vskip 1em
\noindent (c) The von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}=P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P$, acting on the Hilbert space
${\cal K}$ i.e. the range of $P$, is generated by $\{v_k,v^*_k:1 \le k \le d \}''$ and the normal state
$\phi(x)=<\Omega,x \Omega>$ is faithful on the von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}$.

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (d) The self-adjoint part of the commutant of $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ is norm and order isomorphic to the space
of self-adjoint fixed points of the completely positive map $\tau$. The isomorphism takes $X' \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$
onto $PX'P \in {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$, where ${\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K}) = \{ x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \tau(x)=x \}$ and 
$\tau(x)=\sum_kv_kxv^*_k,\;x \in {\cal B}({\cal K})$. Furthermore ${\cal M}' = {\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$.

\vskip 1em
Conversely let ${\cal M}$ be a von-Neumann algebra generated by a family $\{v_k: 1 \le k \le d \}$ of bounded operators
on a Hilbert space ${\cal K}$ so that $\sum_kv_kv_k^*=1$ and the commutant 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal M}'=\{x \in {\cal B}({\cal K}): \sum_k v_kxv_k^*=x \}
\end{equation} 
Then the Popescu dilation $({\cal H},P,S_k,\;1 \le k \le d)$ described in Theorem 2.1 satisfies the following:

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (i) $P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,\;1 \le k \le d \}''$;

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (ii) For any faithful normal $\tau-$invariant state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ there exists a state $\psi$ on ${\cal O}_d$ defined by
$$\psi(s_Is^*_J)=\phi(v_Iv^*_J),\;|I|,|J| < \infty $$
such that the GNS space associated with $({\cal M},\phi)$ is the support projection
for $\psi$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$ satisfying (a)-(d). 

\vskip 1em
Further for a given $\lambda$-invariant state $\psi$, the family $({\cal K},{\cal M},v_k\;1 \le k \le d,\phi)$ satisfying (a)-(d) 
is determined uniquely up to unitary conjugation. 

\vskip 1em
\noindent (e) $\phi$ is a faithful normal $\tau$-invariant state on ${\cal M}$. Furthermore the following statements are equivalent:

\noindent (i) $({\cal O}_d,\lambda,\psi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (ii) $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic;

\noindent (iii) ${\cal M}$ is a factor.

\end{pro} 

\vskip 1em
\begin{proof} 
$\Lambda(P)$ is also a projection in $\pi_{\psi}({\cal O}_d)''$ so that
$\psi_{\Omega}(\Lambda(P))=1$ by invariance property. Thus we have $\Lambda(P) \ge P$ i.e.
$P\Lambda(I-P)P=0$. Hence we have
\begin{equation}
PS^*_kP=S^*_kP
\end{equation}
Moreover by $\lambda$ invariance property we also note that the faithful normal state
$\phi(x)=<\Omega,x\Omega>$ on the von-Neumann algebra ${\cal M}=P\pi_{\psi}({\cal O}_d)''P$
is invariant for the reduced Markov map [Mo1] on ${\cal M}$ given by
\begin{equation}
\tau(x)=P\Lambda(PxP)P
\end{equation}
\vskip 1em
We claim that $\mbox{lim}_{n \uparrow \infty}\Lambda^n(P)= I$. That $\{ \Lambda^n(P): n \ge 1 \}$
is a sequence of increasing projections follows from sub-harmonic property of $P$ and endomorphism
property of $\Lambda$. Let the limiting projection be $Y$. Then $\Lambda(Y)=Y$ and so $Y \in
\{S_k,S^*_k \}'$. Since by our construction, the GNS Hilbert space ${\cal H}_{\pi_{\hat{\omega}}}$ is
generated by $S_IS^*_J\Omega$, $Y$ is a scalar. $Y$ being a non-zero projection, it is
the identity operator in ${\cal H}_{\pi_{\psi}}$.

\vskip 1em
Now it is routine to verify (a) (b) and (c). For the first part of (d) we appeal to Theorem 2.1. For the last part
note that for any invariant element $D$ in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$ there exists an element $X'$ in $\pi({\cal O}_d)'$ so that $PX'P=D$.
Since $P \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$ we note that $(1-P)X'P=0$.
Now since $X' \in \{ S_k,S^*_k \}'$, we verify that $Dv^*_k= PXPS^*_kP=PXS^*_kP=PS^*_kXP=PS^*_kPXP=v^*_kD$. Since $D^* \in
{\cal B}_{\tau}({\cal K})$ we also have $D^*v^*_k=v^*_kD^*$. Thus $D \in \{v_k,v^*_k: 1 \le k \le d \}'={\cal M}'$. Since
$P\pi_{\hat{\omega}}({\cal O}_d)'P=
{\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau}$, we conclude that ${\cal B}({\cal K})_{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M}'$. The reverse inclusion is trivial.
This completes the proof for (d).

\vskip 1em
For the converse part: for (i), since by our assumption and the commutant lifting property self-adjoint elements of the commutant
$\{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}'$ is order isometric with the algebra ${\cal M}'$ via the map $X' \rightarrow PX'P$,
$P \in \{S_k,S^*_k,1 \le k \le d \}''$ by Proposition 4.2 in [BJKW]. For (ii) without loss of generality, we assume
that $\phi(x)=<\Omega,x\Omega>$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$ and $\Omega$ is a cyclic and separating vector for ${\cal M}$.
( otherwise we set state $\psi(s_Is^*_J)=\phi(v_Iv_J^*)$ and consider its GNS representation )
We are left to show that $\Omega$ is a cyclic vector for the representation $\pi(s_i) \rightarrow S_i$. To that end 
let $Y \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$ be the projection on the subspace generated by the vectors $\{S_IS^*_J\Omega:  
|I|,|J| < \infty \}$. Note that, $P$ being an element in $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$, $Y$ also commutes with all the elements of 
$P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P=P {\cal M} P$. Hence $Yx\Omega=x\Omega$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$. Thus $Y \ge P$.  
Since $\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ by our construction, we conclude that $Y=\Lambda_n(Y) 
\ge \Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$. Hence $Y=I$. In other words
$\Omega$ is cyclic for the representation $s_i \rightarrow S_i$. This completes the proof for (ii). 

\vskip 1em
Uniqueness up to unitary isomorphism follows as GNS representation is determined uniquely up to unitary conjugation 
and so its support projection.  

\vskip 1em
The first part of (e) we note that $PS_IS^*_JP=v_Iv_J^*$ for all $|I|,|J| < \infty$ and thus ${\cal M}=P\pi({\cal O}_d)''P$ is the von-Neumann 
algebra generated by $\{v_k,v_k^*:1 \le k \le d \}$ and thus $\tau(x)=P\Lambda(PxP)P$ for all $x \in {\cal M}$. That $\phi$ is 
$\tau(x)=\sum_k v_kxv_k^*$ invariant follows as $\psi$ is $\lambda$-invariant. We are left to prove equivalence of statements (i)-(iii).  

\vskip 1em
By Theorem 3.6 in [Mo1] the Markov semi-group $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$ is ergodic if and
only if $(\pi({\cal O}_d)'',\Lambda,\psi_{\Omega})$ is ergodic ( here we need to recall by (a) that
$\Lambda_n(P) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). By a standard result [Ev, also BJKW] $({\cal M},\tau,\phi)$
is ergodic if and only if there is no non trivial projection $e$ invariant for $\tau$ i.e. ${\cal I}^{\tau} = \{e \in {\cal M}: e^*=e,e^2=e,\tau(e)=e \}=\{0,1 \}$. 
If $\tau(e)=e$ for some projection $e \in {\cal M} $ then $(1-e)\tau(e)(1-e)=0$ and so $ev^*_k(1-e)=0$. Same is true 
if we replace $e$ by $1-e$ as $\tau(1-e)=\tau(1)-\tau(e)=1-e$ and so $(1-e)v^*_ke=0$. Thus $e$ commutes with $v_k,v_k^*$ for all $1 \le k \le d$. 
Hence ${\cal I}^{\tau} \subseteq {\cal M} \bigcap {\cal M}'$. Inequality in the reverse direction is trivial and thus ${\cal I}^{\tau}$ is trivial if and only if ${\cal M}$ is a factor. 
This shows equivalence of (ii) and (iii) follows by a standard result [La,Fr] in non-commutative ergodic theory. This completes the proof.
\end{proof} 

\vskip 1em
The following two propositions are essentially easy adaptations of results proved in [BJKW, Section 6 and Section 7]. These results are  
crucial in our present framework. 

\begin{pro} 
Let $\psi$ be a $\lambda$ invariant factor state on ${\cal O}_d$ and $({\cal H},\pi,\Omega)$
be its GNS representation. Then the following holds:

\noindent (a) The closed subgroup $H=\{z \in S^1: \psi \beta_z =\psi \}$ is equal to 

$$\{z \in S^1: \beta_z \mbox{extends to an automorphism of } \pi({\cal O}_d)'' \} $$ 

\noindent (b) Let ${\cal O}_d^{H}$ be the fixed point sub-algebra in ${\cal O}_d$ under the action of gauge group $\{ \beta_z: z \in H \}$. Then  
$\pi({\cal O}_d^{H})'' = \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''$.

\noindent (c) If $H$ is a finite cyclic group of $k$ many elements and $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''$ is a factor, 
then $\pi({\cal O}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)' \equiv \mathbb{C}^m$ where $1 \le m \le k$.  
\end{pro}

\vskip 1em 
\begin{proof}  
It is simple that $H$ is a closed subgroup. For any fix $z \in H $ we define unitary operator $U_z$ 
extending the map $\pi(x)\Omega \rightarrow \pi(\beta_z(x))\Omega$ and check that the map $X \rightarrow U_zXU^*_z$ extends $\beta_z$ 
to an automorphism of $\pi({\cal O}_d)''$. For the converse we will use the hypothesis that $\psi$ is a $\lambda$-invariant 
factor state and $\beta_z \lambda= \lambda \beta_z$ to guarantee that $\psi \beta_z (X) = {1 \over n} 
\sum_{1 \le k \le n} \psi \lambda^k \beta_z(X) = {1 \over n} \sum_{1 \le k \le n} \psi \beta_z \lambda^k(X) 
\rightarrow \psi(X)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for any $X \in \pi({\cal O}_d)''$, where we have used the same symbol $\beta_z$ 
for the extension. Hence $z \in H$. 

\vskip 1em
In the following instead of working with ${\cal O}_d$ we should be working with the inductive limit $C^*$ algebra and their inductive limit states. 
For simplicity of notation we still use $UHF_d,{\cal O}_d$ for its inductive limit of ${\cal O}_d \rightarrow^{\lambda} {\cal O}_d$ 
and $UHF_d \rightarrow^{\lambda} UHF_d$ respectively and so for its inductive limit states.   

\vskip 1em
Now we aim to prove (b). $H$ being a closed subgroup of $S^1$, it is either entire $S^1$ or a finite subgroup 
$\{exp({ 2i \pi l \over k})|l=0,1,...,k-1 \}$ where the integer $k \ge 1$. If $H=S^1$ we have nothing to prove 
for (b). When $H$ is a finite closed subgroup, we identify $[0,1)$ with $S^1$ by the usual map and note that 
if $\beta_t$ is restricted to $t \in [0,{1 \over k})$, then by scaling we check that $\beta_t$ defines a 
representation of $S^1$ in automorphisms of ${\cal O}^H_d$. Now we consider the direct integral representation 
$\pi'$ defined by
$$\pi'= \int^{\oplus}_{[0,{1 \over k})} dt \pi_{|_{{\cal O}^H_d}} \beta_t $$
of ${\cal O}_d^{H}$ on ${\cal H}_{|_{{\cal O}_d^H}}\otimes L^2([0,{1 \over k})\;)$, where ${\cal H}_{|_{{\cal O}_d^H}}$ is the cyclic
space of $\pi({\cal O}_d^H)$ generated by $\Omega$. That it is indeed direct integral follows as states
$\psi \beta_{t_1}$ and $\psi \beta_{t_2}$ are either same or orthogonal for a factor state $\psi$ (see the proof of Lemma 7.4 in [BJKW] for further details).
Interesting point here to note that the new representation $\pi'$ 
is $(\beta_t)$ co-variant i.e. $\pi' \beta_t=\beta_t \pi' $, hence by simplicity of the $C^*$ algebra ${\cal O}_d$ we 
conclude that $$\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi'({\cal O}_d^{H})''^{\beta_t}$$
 
\vskip 1em
By exploring the hypothesis that $\psi$ is a factor state, 
we also have as in Lemma 6.11 in [BJKW] $I \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;) \subset \pi'({\cal O}_d^H)''$. 
Hence we also have
$$\pi'({\cal O}_d^H)''= \pi({\cal O}_d^H)'' \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;).$$ 
Since $\beta_t$ is acting as translation on $I \otimes L^{\infty}([0,{1 \over k})\;)$ which being 
an ergodic action, we have 
$$\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi({\cal O}_d^{H})'' \otimes 1$$
Since $\pi'(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' \otimes 1$, we conclude 
that $\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)'' = \pi({\cal O}_d^{H})''$. 

\vskip 1em
A proof for the statement (c) follows from Lemma 7.12 in [BJKW]. The original idea of the proof can be 
traced back to Arveson's work on spectrum of an automorphism of a commutative compact group [Ar1]. 
\end{proof}

\vskip 1em
Let $\omega'$ be an $\lambda$-invariant state on the $\mbox{UHF}_d$ sub-algebra of ${\cal O}_d$. Following [BJKW, section 7], 
we consider the set 
$$K_{\omega'}= \{ \psi: \psi \mbox{ is a state on } {\cal O}_d \mbox{ such that } \psi \lambda =
\psi \mbox{ and } \psi_{|\mbox{UHF}_d} = \omega' \}$$

By taking invariant mean on an extension of $\omega'$ to ${\cal O}_d$, we verify that $K_{\omega'}$ is non empty and 
$K_{\omega'}$ is clearly convex and compact in the weak topology. In case $\omega'$ is an ergodic state ( extremal state )
$K_{\omega'}$ is a face in the $\lambda$ invariant states. Before we proceed to the next section here we recall Lemma 7.4 
of [BJKW] in the following proposition.

\vskip 1em 
\begin{pro} Let $\omega'$ be ergodic. Then $\psi \in K_{\omega'}$ is an extremal point in
$K_{\omega'}$ if and only if $\psi$ is a factor state and moreover any other extremal point in $K_{\omega'}$
has the form $\psi \beta_z$ for some $z \in S^1$.
\end{pro} 


\vskip 1em
\begin{proof} 
Though Proposition 7.4 in [BJKW] appeared in a different set up, the same proof goes through for
the present case. We omit the details and refer to the original work for a proof.
\end{proof}

\vskip 1em
\begin{proof} 
First we will prove that $\omega$ is pure if $P$ is also the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$, 
where $\tilde{{\cal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\Omega]$. The support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is $\tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ and thus we also 
have $P = \tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ by our hypothesis. Since $\Lambda^n(P)=\Lambda^n({\cal E}){\cal F} \uparrow {\cal F}$ and now
$\Lambda^n(P)=\tilde{{\cal E}}\Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \uparrow \tilde{{\cal E}}$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, we also have 
${\cal F} = \tilde{{\cal E}}$. Similarly we also have for each $n$, ${\cal E}\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\cal E}})\tilde{{\cal F}}$ 
and thus taking limit we also get ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$.  

\vskip 1em 
So we have $P={\cal E} {\cal F}={\cal E} \tilde{{\cal E}}=Q$. $\tilde{{\cal M}}=P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P$ is cyclic in ${\cal K}$ i.e. 
$[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=[P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P\Omega]= P\tilde{{\cal F}}=P{\cal E}=P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$.  

\vskip 1em 
However $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)) = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ ( for a proof which is a simple 
application of Cuntz relation, we refer to section 5 of [Mo2]). Further $\psi$ being a factor state in $K_{\omega'}$, by Proposition 3.2 $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is a factor. 
In particular we have $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d))\tilde{{\cal F}} = \mathbb{C} \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Thus by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] we conclude that $||\Psi \circ \tilde{\tau}_n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ 
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all normal state $\Psi$ on $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=P \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ and support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ 
is $\tilde{{\cal E}}$ and $P={\cal E}\tilde{{\cal E}}{\cal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
Note that $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0 \subseteq {\cal M}_0'$ where ${\cal M}_0=P\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''P$. Further by Proposition 2.5 
${\cal M}_0 = \{x \in {\cal M}:\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}\;\;\;$ and  $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=\{x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}:
\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}$. Once we set $P_0=[{\cal M}_0\Omega]$ then we also have $P_0=[\tilde{{\cal M}}_0\Omega]$ 
as $[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=P=[{\cal M}\Omega]$ by expending $u_z=\sum_{k \in \hat{H}} z^kP_k$ where $z \rightarrow u_z=
PU_zP$ is a unitary representation of group $H$.      

\vskip 1em
For $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}, y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$ we have  
$$\phi(\tilde{\tau}(x)y)=\sum_k <\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega,x\tilde{v}^*_ky\Omega> = \sum_k <v^*_k\Omega,x y \tilde{v}^*_k\Omega>$$  
(as $v_k^*\Omega=\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega$ )
$$=\sum_k <\Omega, x v_kyv_k^* \Omega>=\phi(x \tau(y))$$
The dual group of $(\tilde{{\cal M}},\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given on the commutant by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}',\tau,\phi)$ where $\tau(x)=\sum_k v_k x v_k^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$. 
where commutant is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$. 
Now moving to $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in the duality relation above, we verify that 
adjoint Markov map of $(\tilde{{\cal M}}_0,\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0,\tau,\phi)$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$, the commutant of $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ 
is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$ and ${\cal K}_0$ is the Hilbert subspace $P_0$ with $\Omega$ as
cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ in ${\cal K}_0$. Thus by Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3], 
there exists a sequence of elements $y_n \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$ such that for each $m \ge 1$, 
$y_{m+n}\tau_n(y) \rightarrow \phi(y)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0 \subseteq {\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$. 
Thus $\omega$ is pure by Proposition 3.5 (e) once we recall ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$ as $P=Q$ 
( and so ${\cal M}'_0 = \tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ ) by Proposition 3.5 (d). This completes the proof of
 purity property of $\omega$. 


\vskip 1em  
In the following we now prove the hardest part of the theorem namely $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ and ${\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}$ if $\omega$ is pure. Proof uses extensively 
the general theory of quasi-equivalent representation of a $C^*$ algebra and we refer [BR1, Chapter 2.4.4] as a general reference.   

\vskip 1em 
We set unitary operator $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}^*_k$. That $V$ is a unitary operator follows by Cuntz's relations and commuting property 
of $(S_i)$ and $(\tilde{S}_i)$. Further a simple computation shows that $V\pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\cal B} = {\cal B}_L \otimes {\cal B}_R$, 
identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ and $\theta$ is the right shift. We also have    
\begin{equation} 
\theta({\cal E})=V {\cal E} V^*= \sum_{k,k'}S_k\tilde{S}^*_k {\cal E} S^*_{k'}\tilde{S}_{k'}=\Lambda({\cal E}) \ge {\cal E}
\end{equation} 
Similarly we also have
\begin{equation} 
\theta(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}} 
\end{equation}
So in particular we have $V(I-{\cal E})V^* \le I-{\cal E}$, i.e. $(I-{\cal E})V^*{\cal E}=0$.  
Also for any $X \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$ we have $V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}X\Omega = 
\tilde{{\cal F}} \sum_k \tilde{S}_k X \tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$ as $S_k^*\Omega 
=\tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$. Thus $(I-\tilde{{\cal F}})V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}=0$ i.e. 
$V\tilde{{\cal F}}V^*=\Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Similarly we also 
have 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\cal E}})=V^*\tilde{{\cal E}}V \ge \tilde{{\cal E}}\;\mbox{and}\; V^* {\cal F} V \ge {\cal F}
\end{equation} 
We also set two family of increasing projections for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ as follows 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal E}_n=V^n {\cal E} (V^n)^*,\;\;\tilde{{\cal F}}_n=V^n\tilde{{\cal F}}(V^n)^*
\end{equation}

\vskip 1em 
Since $\beta_z(V)=V$ for all $z \in H$, $V \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by Proposition 3.4 as $\omega$ is pure. $\omega$ being also a factor state, we have $<f,V^ng> \rightarrow <f,\Omega><\Omega,g>$ as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$ for any $f,g \in \pi({\cal B}_{loc})\Omega$ by Power's criteria [Pow] given in (1). Since such vectors are dense in the Hilbert space topology and the family $\{V^n:n \ge 1\}$ is uniformly bounded, we get $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$.   

\vskip 1em 
For the time being we assume that $H$ is trivial. Otherwise the argument that follows here we can use for the representation $\pi_0$ of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ i.e. $\pi$ restricted to $[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. 

\vskip 1em 
We have following distinct cases: 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 1.} ${\cal E} \neq I \;( \tilde{{\cal E}} \neq I)$. Let ${\cal E}_n \rightarrow {\cal E}_{-\infty}$ as $n \rightarrow -\infty$ and thus $V{\cal E}_{-\infty}V^*={\cal E}_{-\infty}$. We claim that either ${\cal E}_{-\infty} = |\Omega><\Omega|$ or ${\cal E}_{-\infty}$ is a proper infinite dimensional projection i.e. if ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ is a finite projection then ${\cal E}_{- \infty}=|\Omega><\Omega|$. Suppose not then the finite subspace is shift invariant. In particular there exists a unit  vector $f$ orthogonal to $\Omega$ such that $Vf=zf$ for some $z \in S^1$ and this contradicts weak mixing property i.e. $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology proved above as point spectrum of $V$ has only $1$ with spectral multiplicity $1$. 

\vskip 1em 
If ${\cal E}_{-\infty}$ is infinite dimensional we can get a unitary operator $U_0$ from 
$F_0=\tilde{{\cal H}} \otimes_{{\cal K}} {\cal H}$ onto ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ and 
via the unitary map we can get a sequence of increasing projections $U_0{\cal E}_nU^*_0$ in ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ and note that $U_0{\cal E}_nU_0^*=V^nU_0 {\cal E} U_0^*(V^n)^*$. Note that if ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ is infinite dimension the process will not stop in finite step. Thus we have $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{{\cal E}}} F(k)$ where the index set is either singleton or infinity and each $F(k)$ will give a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$, where $F(1)
=F_0-{\cal E}_{-\infty}$. Further $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ being a simple $C^*$-algebra, each such imprimitivity system 
is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ [Mo3,section 4]: We fix a nonzero $f \in {\cal E}-\theta^{-1}({\cal E}) \neq 0$ otherwise ${\cal E}=I$ as $\theta^n({\cal E}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. $\pi_f:x \rightarrow \theta^{-1}(x)f$ gives a representation of $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d={\cal B}_L$ and we check that $[\pi_f(\theta^{-1}({\cal B}_L)''f] \le {\cal E}-\theta^{-1}({\cal E})$ 
as $f \perp [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\cal B}_R)')\Omega] \ge [\theta^{-1}(\pi({\cal B}_L))\Omega]$. Thus simplicity 
ensures that ${\cal E} - \theta^{-1}({\cal E})$ is a projection of dimension $\aleph_0$. Further $n_{\cal E}$ is either $1$
or $\aleph_0$ since $F_0$ is separable.   

\vskip 1em 
Since $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is also a proper projection, same argument is valid for $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ with $\tilde{{\cal F}}_{-\infty}=
\mbox{lim}_{n \rightarrow -\infty} \theta^n(\tilde{{\cal F}})$ i.e. we can write $F_0 \ominus \Omega = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n_{\tilde{{\cal F}}}} \tilde{H}(k)$, where each $\tilde{H}(k)$ give rises to a system of imprimitivity with respect to $V$ where each system of imprimitivity is of Mackey index $\aleph_0$ where $\tilde{F}(1) = F_0-\tilde{{\cal F}}_{-\infty}$ 
and $n_{\tilde{{\cal F}}}$ is either $1$ or $\aleph_0$.        

\vskip 1em 
In the following we use temporary notation $H$ for Hilbert subspace $F_0$. For a cardinal number $n$, we 
amplify a representation $\pi:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(H)$ of the $C^*$ algebra ${\cal B}$ to $n$ fold direct sum 
$n\pi=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } \pi_k $ acting on $nH=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n } H_k$  defining by 
$$n\pi(x) (\oplus \zeta_k) = \oplus (\pi(x)\zeta_k)$$ 
where $\pi_k = \pi$ is the representation of ${\cal B}=\mbox{UHF}_d \otimes \tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d$ 
on $H_k=H$ where $H =[\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)\Omega]$. We also 
extend $\bar{\tilde{F}} = \oplus \tilde{F}_{\alpha}$, $\bar{E} = \oplus E_{\alpha}$ and $\bar{V}=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n} V_k$ respectively. We also set notation $\Omega_k=\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}\delta^k_j\Omega$. 

\vskip 1em 
Thus by Mackey's theorem, there exists a cardinal number $n \in \aleph_0$ and a unitary operator $U: nH \rightarrow nH$ so that 
$\bar{V}=U\bar{V}U^*$ and $\bar{{\cal E}}=U\bar{\tilde{{\cal F}}}U^*$. We set a representation 
$\pi^U:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(nH)$ by $\pi^U(x)= Un\pi(x)U^*$
and rewrite the above identity as 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] = \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^U_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$
where $\pi^U_k(x)=U\pi_k(x)U^*$. Note that by our construction we 
can ensure $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ for all $1 \le k \le n$ as the operator 
intertwining between two imprimitivity systems are acting on the orthogonal 
subspace of the projection generated by vectors $\{\Omega_k:1 \le k \le n\}$. 

\vskip 1em 
We claim ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. Suppose not i.e. $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}$. In such a case we 
have
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega_k]$$
Alternatively 
$$\oplus_{1 \le k \le n}[\pi_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k] < \oplus_{1 \le k \le n}
[\pi^u_k(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega_k]$$

\vskip 1em 
Thus in principle we can repeat our construction now with $\pi^U$ and so we 
get a strict partial ordered set of quasi-equivalent representation of ${\cal B}$. 
In the following we now aim to employ formal set theory to bring a contradiction 
on our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
To that end we need to deal with more then one representation of ${\cal B}$. For the rest of the proof we reset notation $\pi_0$ for $\pi$ used for the pure representation of 
${\cal B}$ in $H_0 =[\pi_0({\cal B})\Omega_0]$ where $\Omega_0$ is the cyclic vector, the reset notation for $\Omega$. Let ${\cal P}$ be the collection of representation $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega)$ 
quasi-equivalent to $\pi_0:{\cal B} \rightarrow {\cal B}(H_0)$ with a shift invariant vector state $\omega(x)=<\Omega,\pi(x)\Omega>$ i.e. $\omega(\pi(\theta(x))=\omega(\pi(x))$. So there exists 
minimal cardinal numbers $n_{\pi},n_0(\pi)$ so that $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}$ is unitary equivalent to $n_0(\pi)\pi_0$. Thus for such an element $(\pi,H_{\pi},\Omega_{\pi})$ we can associate 
two cardinal numbers $n_{\pi}$ and $n_0(\pi)$ and without loss of generality we assume that $H_{\pi} \subseteq n_0(\pi)H_0$ and $n_{\pi}H_{\pi}=n_0(\pi)H_0.$  $\pi_0$ being a pure 
representation, any element $\pi \in {\cal P}$ is a type-I factor representation of ${\cal B}$. The interesting point here that $\displaystyle{\oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P} }}\pi$ is also an element in ${\cal P}$ 
with associated cardinal numbers $\sum_{\pi} n_{\pi}$ and $\sum_{\pi} n_0(\pi)$. We say $(\pi_1,H_{\pi_1},\Omega^1) \prec (\pi_2,H_{\pi_2},\Omega^2)$ if there exists an 
isometry $U:n_{\pi_1} H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_2} H_{\pi_2}$ so that 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C1) For each $1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} $ we have 
$U \Omega^1_{\alpha} = \Omega^2_{\alpha'}$ for some 
$1 \le \alpha' \le n_{\pi_2}$;        

\noindent (C2) $n_{\pi_2}\pi_2(x)E'_2 = U n_{\pi_1}\pi_1(x) U^* $ where ${\cal E}'_2 \in n_{\pi_2}\pi_2({\cal B})'$; 
 
\noindent (C3) $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^1_{\alpha}] < \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\mbox{UHF}_d)'\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$.

\vskip 1em 
In the inequality we explicitly used that both Hilbert spaces are subspaces of $nH_0$ for some possibly larger cardinal 
number $n$. That the partial order is non-reflexive follows as $(\pi,H,\Omega) \prec (\pi,H,\Omega)$ contradicts 
(C3) as $I=E_2'$. Partial order property follows easily. If $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ and $\pi_2 \prec \pi_3$ then $\pi_1 \prec \pi_3$. 
If $U_{12}$ and $U_{23}$ are isometric operators that satisfies (C1)-(C3) respectively, then $U_{13}=U_{23}U_{12}$ will 
do the job for $\pi_1$ and $\pi_3$. Thus $\pi^U \in {\cal P}$ and by our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\cal F}} \neq {\cal E}$ we also 
check that $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. Thus going via the isomorphism we also check that for a given element $\pi \in {\cal P}$ there exists 
an element $\pi' \in {\cal P}$ so that $\pi \prec \pi'$. Thus ${\cal P}_0$ is a non empty set and has at least one infinite chain containing $\pi_0$.
 
\vskip 1em 
However by Hausdorff maximality theorem there exists a non-empty maximal totally ordered subset ${\cal P}_0$ of ${\cal P}$ 
containing $\pi_0$. We claim that $\pi_{max} = \oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} \pi$ on $H_{\pi_{max}}=\oplus_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} H_{\pi} $ is an upper bound in ${\cal P}_0$. That $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}$ is obvious. Further given an element $(H_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_1) \in {\cal P}_0$ there exists an element $(H_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_2) \in {\cal P}_0$ so that $\pi_1 \prec \pi_2$ by our starting remark as $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$. By extending isometry $U_{12}$ to an isometry from $H_{\pi_1} \rightarrow n_{\pi_{max}} H_{\pi_{max}}$ trivially we get the required isometry that satisfies (C1),(C2) and (C3) where cardinal numbers $n_{\pi_{max}} = \sum_{\pi \in {\cal P}_0} n_{\pi} \in \aleph$. Thus by maximal property of ${\cal P}_0$ we have $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}_0$. This brings a contradiction as by our construction $(\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega) \prec (\pi_{max},H_{\pi_{max}},\Omega)$ as $\pi_{max} \in {\cal P}_0$ but partial order is strict. This contradicts our starting hypothesis that $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}$. This completes the proof that $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ when ${\cal E} \neq I$. By symmetry of the argument we also get ${\cal F}=\tilde{{\cal E}}$ when $\tilde{{\cal E}} < 1$.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Case 2:} ${\cal E}=I \;(\tilde{{\cal E}}=I)$. We need to show $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I\;({\cal F}=I)$ respectively. Suppose not and assume that both $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is a proper non-zero projection. 

\vskip 1em 
We set projection $G$ on the closed linear span of elements in the subspaces $[\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]$ for all $n \ge 0$. We recall that $\theta(X)=VXV^*$ 
where $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}_k^*$ and $\theta^{-1}(X)=\tilde{\Lambda}(X)$ 
for $X \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$. Thus we have 
$$V^*\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\cal F})V^*\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''V\Omega$$
$$=\theta^{-n-1}({\cal F}) \tilde{\Lambda}(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega.$$
Thus $(1-G)V^*G=0$ i.e. $\theta(G) \ge G$. It is also clear that $\tilde{{\cal F}} \le G$ 
as the defining sequence of subspaces of $G$ goes to precisely $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ ( recall 
that $\theta^{-n}({\cal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}_n({\cal F}) \uparrow I$ strongly as $n \uparrow \infty$ ). Once more we have 
$\theta^n(G) \ge \theta^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \uparrow I$ as $n \uparrow 
\infty$.  

\vskip 1em 
If $G$ is a proper projection we can follow the steps as in the case 1 to find a unitary operator 
$U:nH \rightarrow nH$ with $U\Omega_k=\Omega_k$ and $U\bar{V}U^*=\bar{V}$ so that $U\bar{G}U^*=\bar{\tilde{{\cal F}}}$. 
We consider the subset ${\cal P}_G$ of elements in ${\cal P}$ for which ${\cal E}_{\pi}=1$ and 
$\{\theta^{-n}({\cal F}_{\pi}):n \ge 0 \}$ commutes with $\tilde{{\cal F}}_{\pi}$ 
and modify the strict partial ordering by modifying (C3) as  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent (C3') $\oplus_{1 \le \alpha \le n_{\pi_1} }[\pi^{\alpha}_1(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^1_{\alpha}] <  \oplus_{1 \le 
\alpha \le n_{\pi_2}}[\pi^{\alpha}_2(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega^2_{\alpha}]E'_2$

\noindent So we also get $\pi^U \in {\cal P}_G$ and $\pi_0 \prec \pi^U$ and going along the same line we conclude that 
$G=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. Thus we conclude that $G$ is either equal to $1$ or $G=\tilde{{\cal F}}$. 

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 1 of case 2:} If $G=I$ then ${\cal F} G = {\cal F}$ and so $[{\cal F}\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''\Omega]={\cal F}$ as $\theta^{-n}({\cal F}) \ge {\cal F}$. 
Thus $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge {\cal F}$. So $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge \tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F})$ for all $n \ge 1$ and taking limit we get $\tilde{{\cal F}} \ge I$ i.e. $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I$. 
This contradicts our starting assumption that $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is a proper projection.  

\vskip 1em 
\noindent {\bf Sub-case 2 of case 2:} Now we consider the case $G=\tilde{{\cal F}} < I$. In such a case we have 
$(1- \tilde{{\cal F}})\theta^{-n}({\cal F})\tilde{{\cal F}}=0$ and so $\theta^{-n}({\cal F})$ commutes with $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ for all $n \ge 0$. 

\vskip 1em 
First we rule out the simplest possibility in the present situation for ${\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} = |\Omega><\Omega|$. If so then $\omega$ is
a Bernoulli state and a proof follows once we compute the following using the property $\Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$ i.e.
$\tilde{{\cal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}$ 
and commuting property of ${\cal F}$ with $\pi(s_i)^*$ to get some scalars $\bar{\lambda_i}$ such
that 
$$\bar{\lambda}_i= {\cal F}\tilde{{\cal F}}\pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F} = \pi(s_i)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F}$$
and so 
$$\omega(s_Is_J^*)=<\Omega,\pi(s_I) \pi(s_J)^*\Omega>$$
$$=<\Omega, {\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} \pi(s_I)\pi(s_J)^*\tilde{{\cal F}}{\cal F} \Omega>$$
$$=\lambda_I\lambda_J^*$$
The inductive limit state $\omega$ on ${\cal B}$, give rises to a pure state once restricted to ${\cal B}_R$ and thus we have 
${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$ by Haag duality when $\pi({\cal B}_R)''$ is a type-I factor. This contradicts our starting assumption that ${\cal E}=I$.   

\vskip 1em 
Now we set projection ${\cal F}'$ defined by 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal F}'={\cal F}-{\cal F}\tilde{{\cal F}}+|\Omega><\Omega|
\end{equation} 
and check by commuting property of $\tilde{{\cal F}}$ with ${\cal F}$ that 
$$ 
{\cal F}'\theta^{-1}({\cal F}'){\cal F}' = (I-\tilde{{\cal F}}){\cal F}\theta^{-1}({\cal F})(I-\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\cal F}}))(I-\tilde{{\cal F}}){\cal F} 
+ |\Omega><\Omega|$$ 
$$= {\cal F}(I-\tilde{{\cal F}}) + |\Omega><\Omega|={\cal F}'$$ 
where we have used $\theta^{-1}({\cal F}) = \tilde{\Lambda}({\cal F}) \ge {\cal F},\; \theta({\cal F}) \le {\cal F}$ and  
$\theta(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$. 
Thus we get 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}({\cal F}') \ge {\cal F}'
\end{equation}                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     

\vskip 1em 
We also rule out the possibility that ${\cal F} \tilde{{\cal F}} = {\cal F}$. If so then ${\cal F} \le \tilde{{\cal F}}$ and $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F}) \le 
\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) = \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Taking limit we get $\tilde{{\cal F}}=I$ as $\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F}) \uparrow I$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. 
This brings a contradiction to our hypothesis.  
  
\vskip 1em 
So we have in particular ${\cal F}' <  {\cal F} \le I$ and ${\cal F}' - |\Omega><\Omega| \neq 0$. Now we will rule out the possibility of ${\cal F}=I$ under our hypothesis $\tilde{{\cal F}} < {\cal E}=I$. 
Suppose so i.e. ${\cal F}=I$, then $\tilde{{\cal E}}=I$ since $\tilde{{\cal E}} \ge {\cal F}$. Then $Q={\cal E} \tilde{{\cal E}} = {\cal E} = {\cal E} {\cal F}=P$. Thus by Proposition 3.5 (e) we get $\pi({\cal O}_d)'=

We also have $\theta^{-1}({\cal F}') \ge {\cal F}'$ and $\theta^{-1}({\cal F}) \ge {\cal F}$. Thus we can follow the steps of Case-1 with elements ${\cal F}',{\cal F},\theta^{-1}$ replacing the role of $\tilde{{\cal F}},{\cal E},\theta$ 
to get a unitary operator $U:nH \rightarrow nH$ so that $U\bar{V}=\bar{V}U$ and $U\bar{{\cal F}}U^*=\bar{{\cal F}'}$ for a 
cardinal number $n$.

Now we consider a further subset ${\cal P}_{G'}$ of ${\cal P}_G$ consist of quasi-equivalent representations $\pi$ to $\pi_0$ 
of ${\cal B}$ where $\pi$ admits the additional property: ${\cal F}_{\pi} < I, {\cal E}_{\pi}=I$ and $\{\theta^{-n}(\tilde{{\cal F}_{\pi}}): n \ge 0 \}$ 
commutes with ${\cal F}_{\pi}$ with the strict partial ordering $({\cal H}_{\pi_1},\pi_1,\Omega_{\pi_1}) \prec ({\cal H}_{\pi_2},\pi_2,\Omega_{\pi_2})$ 
given by modifying condition (C3') as

state of $({\cal B}_R,\psi_R) \rightarrow^{\lambda_n} ({\cal B}_R,\psi_R)$ where $(\lambda_n:n \ge 0)$ is the canonical semi-group of right shifts on ${\cal B}_R$. Pure states on a $\mbox{UHF}$ algebra are studied in the general framework of [Pow]. Such a situation has been investigated also in detail at various degrees of generality in [BJP] and [BJKW] motivated by the development a $C^*$ algebraic method in the study of iterative function systems and its associated wavelet theory. One interesting result in [BJP] says that any translation invariant pure state on ${\cal B}_R$ is also a product state and the canonical endomorphism associated with two such states are unitary equivalent. However such a statement is not true for two translation invariant pure states on ${\cal B}$ as their restriction to ${\cal B}_R$ need not be isomorphic. Theorem 3.4 in [Mo4] says that $\omega_R$ is either a type-I or a type-III factor state on ${\cal B}_R$. Both type of factors are known to exist in the literature of quantum statistical mechanics [BR vol-II,Si,Ma1]. Thus the classification problem of translation dynamics on ${\cal B}$ with invariant pure states on ${\cal B}$ up to unitary isomorphism is a delicate one. In this context one interesting problem that remain open is whether mean entropy [Ru] is an invariance for translation dynamics.   

\vskip 1em 
Since a $\theta$ invariant state $\omega$ on ${\cal B}$ is completely determined by its restriction $\omega_R$ to ${\cal B}_R$, in principle it is possible to describe various properties of $\omega$ including purity by studying their restriction $\omega_R$. 
Theorem 3.2 in [Mo3] gives a precise answer: $\omega$ is pure if and only if there exists a sequence of positive contractive elements $x_n \in {\cal M}$ such that 
$$x_n \rightarrow I,\;\;x_{m+n}\tau_n(x) \rightarrow \phi(x)I$$ 
in strong operator topology for all $x \in {\cal M}$ and $m \ge 1$. As an application of this result, we prove that (e) implies (f). 
This statement can be taken as the correct version of Theorem 7.1 of [BJKW]. Theorem 7.1 in [BJKW] has aimed towards a sufficient condition on Popescu elements ${\cal P}$ for purity of the translation invariant state. However the statement and its proof are faulty as certain argument used in the proof is not time reversal symmetric and a factor state with Popescu elements on support projection satisfies the conditions of the statement of Theorem 7.1. One natural remedy to add additional hypothesis that (e) holds. In particular Lemma 7.6 in [BJKW] needs that additional assumption related to the support projection of the dual state $\tilde{\psi} \in K_{\tilde{\omega}}$. Besides this additional structure proof of Lemma 7.8 in [BJKW] is also not complete unless we find a proof for $\tilde{{\cal M}}={\cal M}'$ ( we retained same notations here in the text) for such a factor state $\omega$. Such a problem could have been solved if there were any method which shows directly that Takesaki's conditional [Ta] expectation exists from ${\cal M}'$ onto $\tilde{{\cal M}}$. For von-Neumann algebras ${\cal N} \subseteq {\cal M}$, a normal unital completely positive map $E_c:{\cal M} \rightarrow {\cal N}$ is called 
{\it normal conditional expectation } if 
\begin{equation} 
E_c(yxz)=yE_c(x)z
\end{equation}
for all $y,z \in {\cal N}$ and $x \in {\cal M}$. 
A theorem of Takesaki's [Ta, also see AcC] says that conditional expectation $E_c$ preserving a faithful normal state $\phi$ on ${\cal M}$ exists if and only if the modular group $\sigma=(\sigma_t:t \in \mathbb{R})$ 
associated with $\phi$, which preserves ${\cal M}$, also preserves ${\cal N}$, i.e. $\sigma_t(x) \in {\cal N}$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in {\cal N}$. Thus main body of the proof for Theorem 7.1 even with the 
additional natural hypothesis $p_0=q_0$, in [BJKW] is incomplete. 

\vskip 1em 
Besides the proof of (e) implies (f), other implication follows along with while we will prove the hardest part of this theorem namely (f) implies (c) i.e. purity implies Haag duality property (16). For the proof 
we have explored the set of representation of ${\cal B}$ quasi-equivalent to $\pi_{\omega}$ and equip it with a strict partial ordering depending on our situation to prove Haag duality. Mackey's system of imprimitivity [Mac] 
plays a crucial role even though a pure state not necessarily give rise to a Mackey's system of imprimitivity generated by the support projection $e_0$ with respect to shift. Though we have worked here with amalgamated representation 
of $\tilde{{\cal O}}_d \otimes {\cal O}_d$ in [BJKW], it seems that just for Haag duality one can avoid doing so. It seems that the underlining group $\mathbb{Z}$ can easily be replaced by $\mathbb{Z}^k$ for some $k \ge 2$ and 
wedge duality for a pointed cone can be proved by following the same ideas. We defer this line of analysis leaving it for work as its relation with problems in quantum spin 
chain in higher dimensional lattice needs some additional structure. We also defer application of Haag duality property in studying symmetry and correlation of a translation invariant pure state to another
paper [Mo5].  

\vskip 1em
The paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we study Popescu's dilation associated with a translation invariant state on Cuntz algebra ${\cal O}_d$ and review `commutant lifting theorem' investigated in [BJKW]. 
The proof presented here remove the murky part of the proof of Theorem 5.1 in [BJKW]. In section 3 we explore both the notion of Kolmogorov's shift and its intimate relation with Mackey's imprimitivity system 
to explore a duality argument introduced in [BJKW]. We find a useful necessary and sufficient condition (Theorem 1.1 (a) ) in terms of support projection of Cuntz's state for a translation invariant factor state 
$\omega$ on ${\cal B}$ to be pure. The criterion on support projection is crucial for our main mathematical result Theorem 3.6. 

\begin{rem} 
The paper ``On Haag Duality for Pure States of Quantum Spin Chain'' 
by authors: M. Keyl, Taku Matsui, D. Schlingemann, R. F. Werner, Rev. Math. Phys. 20:707-724,2008 has an incomplete proof for Haag duality property as Lemma 4.3 in that paper has a faulty argument.   
\end{rem}

\begin{proof} 
First we will prove that $\omega$ is pure if $P$ is also the support projection of the state $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$, 
where $\tilde{{\cal F}}=[\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\Omega]$. The support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''\tilde{{\cal F}}$ is $\tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ and thus we also 
have $P = \tilde{{\cal E}}\tilde{{\cal F}}$ by our hypothesis. Since $\Lambda^n(P)=\Lambda^n({\cal E}){\cal F} \uparrow {\cal F}$ and now
$\Lambda^n(P)=\tilde{{\cal E}}\Lambda^n(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \uparrow \tilde{{\cal E}}$ as $n \uparrow \infty$, we also have 
${\cal F} = \tilde{{\cal E}}$. Similarly we also have for each $n$, ${\cal E}\tilde{\Lambda}^n({\cal F})=\tilde{\Lambda}^n(\tilde{{\cal E}})\tilde{{\cal F}}$ 
and thus taking limit we also get ${\cal E}=\tilde{{\cal F}}$.  

\vskip 1em 
So we have $P={\cal E} {\cal F}={\cal E} \tilde{{\cal E}}=Q$. $\tilde{{\cal M}}=P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P$ is cyclic in ${\cal K}$ i.e. 
$[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=[P\pi(\tilde{{\cal O}}_d)''P\Omega]= P\tilde{{\cal F}}=P{\cal E}=P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$.  

\vskip 1em 
However $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)) = \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'' \bigcap \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)'$ ( for a proof which is a simple 
application of Cuntz relation, we refer to section 5 of [Mo2]). Further $\psi$ being a factor state in $K_{\omega'}$, by Proposition 3.2 $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ is a factor. 
In particular we have $\bigcap_{n \rightarrow \infty} \tilde{\Lambda}^n(\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d))\tilde{{\cal F}} = \mathbb{C} \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Thus by Proposition 1.1 in [Ar2] we conclude that $||\Psi \circ \tilde{\tau}_n -\phi|| \rightarrow 0$ 
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all normal state $\Psi$ on $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=P \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''P$ as $\tilde{{\cal F}}={\cal E}$ and support projection of $\psi$ in $\pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d)''$ 
is $\tilde{{\cal E}}$ and $P={\cal E}\tilde{{\cal E}}{\cal E}$. 

\vskip 1em 
Note that $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0 \subseteq {\cal M}_0'$ where ${\cal M}_0=P\pi(\mbox{UHF}_d)''P$. Further by Proposition 2.5 
${\cal M}_0 = \{x \in {\cal M}:\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}\;\;\;$ and  $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0=\{x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}:
\beta_z(x)=x;z \in H \}$. Once we set $P_0=[{\cal M}_0\Omega]$ then we also have $P_0=[\tilde{{\cal M}}_0\Omega]$ 
as $[\tilde{{\cal M}}\Omega]=P=[{\cal M}\Omega]$ by expending $u_z=\sum_{k \in \hat{H}} z^kP_k$ where $z \rightarrow u_z=
PU_zP$ is a unitary representation of group $H$.      

\vskip 1em
For $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}, y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$ we have  
$$\phi(\tilde{\tau}(x)y)=\sum_k <\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega,x\tilde{v}^*_ky\Omega> = \sum_k <v^*_k\Omega,x y \tilde{v}^*_k\Omega>$$  
(as $v_k^*\Omega=\tilde{v}^*_k\Omega$ )
$$=\sum_k <\Omega, x v_kyv_k^* \Omega>=\phi(x \tau(y))$$
The dual group of $(\tilde{{\cal M}},\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given on the commutant by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}',\tau,\phi)$ where $\tau(x)=\sum_k v_k x v_k^*$ for $x \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'$. 
where commutant is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K})$. 
Now moving to $\{\beta_z: z \in H \}$ invariant elements in the duality relation above, we verify that 
adjoint Markov map of $(\tilde{{\cal M}}_0,\tilde{\tau},\phi)$ is given by 
$(\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0,\tau,\phi)$ where $\tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$, the commutant of $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ 
is taken in ${\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$ and ${\cal K}_0$ is the Hilbert subspace $P_0$ with $\Omega$ as
cyclic and separating vector for $\tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ in ${\cal K}_0$. Thus by Theorem 2.4 in [Mo3], 
there exists a sequence of elements $y_n \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0$ such that for each $m \ge 1$, 
$y_{m+n}\tau_n(y) \rightarrow \phi(y)1$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$ for all $y \in \tilde{{\cal M}}'_0 \subseteq {\cal B}({\cal K}_0)$. 
Thus $\omega$ is pure by Proposition 3.5 (e) once we recall ${\cal M}'=\tilde{{\cal M}}$ as $P=Q$ 
( and so ${\cal M}'_0 = \tilde{{\cal M}}_0$ ) by Proposition 3.5 (d). This completes the proof of
 purity property of $\omega$.

\vskip 1em 
We set unitary operator $V=\sum_k S_k\tilde{S}^*_k$. That $V$ is a unitary operator follows by Cuntz's relations and commuting property 
of $(S_i)$ and $(\tilde{S}_i)$. Further a simple computation shows that $V\pi(x)V^*=\pi(\theta(x))$ for all $x \in {\cal B} = {\cal B}_L \otimes {\cal B}_R$, 
identified with $\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d$ and $\theta$ is the right shift. We also have    
\begin{equation} 
\theta({\cal E})=V {\cal E} V^*= \sum_{k,k'}S_k\tilde{S}^*_k {\cal E} S^*_{k'}\tilde{S}_{k'}=\Lambda({\cal E}) \ge {\cal E}
\end{equation} 
Similarly we also have
\begin{equation} 
\theta(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}} 
\end{equation}
So in particular we have $V(I-{\cal E})V^* \le I-{\cal E}$, i.e. $(I-{\cal E})V^*{\cal E}=0$.  
Also for any $X \in \pi({\cal O}_d)'$ we have $V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}X\Omega = 
\tilde{{\cal F}} \sum_k \tilde{S}_k X \tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$ as $S_k^*\Omega 
=\tilde{S}_k^*\Omega$. Thus $(I-\tilde{{\cal F}})V^*\tilde{{\cal F}}=0$ i.e. 
$V\tilde{{\cal F}}V^*=\Lambda(\tilde{{\cal F}}) \ge \tilde{{\cal F}}$. Similarly we also 
have 
\begin{equation} 
\theta^{-1}(\tilde{{\cal E}})=V^*\tilde{{\cal E}}V \ge \tilde{{\cal E}}\;\mbox{and}\; V^* {\cal F} V \ge {\cal F}
\end{equation} 
We also set two family of increasing projections for all natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ as follows 
\begin{equation} 
{\cal E}_n=V^n {\cal E} (V^n)^*,\;\;\tilde{{\cal F}}_n=V^n\tilde{{\cal F}}(V^n)^*
\end{equation}

\vskip 1em 
Since $\beta_z(V)=V$ for all $z \in H$, $V \in \pi(\tilde{\mbox{UHF}}_d \otimes \mbox{UHF}_d)''$ by Proposition 3.4 as $\omega$ is pure. $\omega$ being also a factor state, we have $<f,V^ng> \rightarrow <f,\Omega><\Omega,g>$ as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$ for any $f,g \in \pi({\cal B}_{loc})\Omega$ by Power's criteria [Pow] given in (1). Since such vectors are dense in the Hilbert space topology and the family $\{V^n:n \ge 1\}$ is uniformly bounded, we get $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology as $n \rightarrow + \mbox{or} - \infty$.

\vskip 1em

We claim that either ${\cal E}_{-\infty} = |\Omega><\Omega|$ or ${\cal E}_{-\infty}$ is a proper infinite dimensional projection i.e. if ${\cal E}_{- \infty}$ is a finite projection then ${\cal E}_{- \infty}=|\Omega><\Omega|$. Suppose not then the finite subspace is shift invariant. In particular there exists a unit  vector $f$ orthogonal to $\Omega$ such that $Vf=zf$ for some $z \in S^1$ and this contradicts weak mixing property i.e. $V^n \rightarrow |\Omega><\Omega|$ in weak operator topology proved above as point spectrum of $V$ has only $1$ with spectral multiplicity $1$. 

\vskip 1em
